You have built Sam’s value panel end to end — linked with validate= on every merge, lagged with merge_asof and proved no peeking with the assertion, run the survivorship smell test, winsorized by date, probed missingness, and emitted the full build log. Now extend it:

Rerun the machinery on Maya’s HMDA-style data. Synthesize a mortgage-application table with applicant_income Missing Not At Random — make income missing more often for denied applications. Then redo the Section 6 probe: the groupby("income_missing")["denied"].mean() should now differ sharply between groups. What does that tell you about dropna()? Build the crosswalk yourself (there is no CCM for HMDA).
Break the look-ahead guard on purpose. Change direction="backward" to direction="forward" in the merge_asof and confirm the no-look-ahead assert fires. This is the one assertion you should never ship without — feel how it catches the bug a backtest never would.
Winsorize or not? Add Devon’s daily crypto returns (a single day can move 40%). Decide: cap at 1/99, model the fat tail, or leave it — and defend the choice against the principle that the variable which is the phenomenon should not be capped away. Re-winsorize bm at 5/95 instead of 1/99 and watch how much the mean moves; that sensitivity is exactly why you fix the cutoff before you look at the result.

title: nb7.5 — First-Look Regressions: Frozen Until the PAP Is Filed
text:
1. The analysis panel (schema like the nb7.4 output)
Week 7, Chapter 7.5 companion. Maya runs the first estimate of her primary specification — once.
This is the most disciplined notebook in the whole camp, and the discipline is the point. By now Maya has done everything Week 7 asked: she generated her idea (7.1), pulled and documented her HMDA-style data (7.2), filed a pre-analysis plan as a tagged commit (7.3), built a clean analysis dataset (7.4), and written the identification memo whose one assumption her headline number rests on (7.5). Only now may she look at the result.
The notebook embodies one rule, the rule that the whole week was built to enforce:
Not the version that gives the prettiest star. Not the clustering level that tightens the t-stat. The one specification she committed to before she could see a coefficient. Chapter 7.3 showed why: with the data already in hand she could peek, so the only thing standing between her and the garden of forking paths is a plan she froze in advance. This notebook is the technological enforcement of that freeze — a gate that refuses to run the regression until PAP_FILED is True.
We do this on a synthetic panel with a known true effect, exactly as the Week 4 DiD notebooks did, for one reason: when you build the world yourself, you know the right answer, so you can check that an honestly-run primary specification — clustered standard errors and all — recovers the planted effect. On real data you never get that luxury; here we use it to prove the machinery is honest.
We load the analysis dataset Maya built in nb7.4. Here we generate it in-notebook so the notebook is self-contained and reproducible, but the schema deliberately matches what a real nb7.4 build emits: one row per county–year, with a treatment cohort, the outcome, the named controls, and the cluster key.
The setting is the fair-lending DiD of Chapter 7.5’s worked memo. Some states adopt a fair-lending examination program in a known year; never-adopting states are the clean controls. The outcome is the county-level minority–white mortgage-denial gap in percentage points (denial rate for minority applicants minus the rate for white applicants). The program, where active, narrows the gap — so the planted true effect is negative.
We write the data-generating process (DGP) as the two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) model run forward, in the notation of CONVENTIONS §3:
\texttt{gap}_{it} = \underbrace{\alpha_i}_{\text{county level}} + \underbrace{\lambda_t}_{\text{year shock}}
+ \underbrace{\tau \cdot \texttt{post\_treat}_{it}}_{\text{the planted effect}}
+ \mathbf{x}_{it}'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon_{it},
where \texttt{post\_treat}_{it}=1 once county i’s state has an active program, \tau is the true ATT we plant, \alpha_i is the county fixed effect, \lambda_t the year fixed effect, and \mathbf{x}_{it} the applicant-composition controls. The county and year fixed effects absorb \alpha_i and \lambda_t; if our spec is honest, the coefficient on the treatment indicator should land on \tau.
# --- Planted truth and panel dimensions ---------------------------------
TAU_TRUE   = -1.80          # the programs NARROW the denial gap by 1.8 pp (the effect we must recover)
YEARS      = list(range(2014, 2024))            # 10 years
N_STATES   = 30             # 30 states -> 30 clusters (treatment varies at the STATE level)
COUNTIES_PER_STATE = 8      # 240 counties, ~2,400 county-year rows
GAMMA_INCOME = -0.9         # higher applicant income -> smaller raw gap
GAMMA_LTV    =  1.2         # higher loan-to-value     -> larger  raw gap
SIGMA        =  0.8         # idiosyncratic county-year noise (sd)

# Half the states adopt; adoption YEAR is staggered across a couple of cohorts.
adopt_cohort = {}                       # state -> year program takes effect (np.nan = never)
for s in range(N_STATES):
    if   s < 8:   adopt_cohort[s] = 2018
    elif s < 15:  adopt_cohort[s] = 2020
    else:         adopt_cohort[s] = np.nan      # never-adopters = clean controls

# State-level mean shift in the baseline gap (some states just have wider gaps).
state_level = {s: rng.normal(0.0, 1.0) for s in range(N_STATES)}
# Year shocks common to all counties (national mortgage-market conditions).
year_shock  = {t: 0.10 * (t - 2014) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.3) for t in YEARS}

rows = []
for s in range(N_STATES):
    G = adopt_cohort[s]
    for c in range(COUNTIES_PER_STATE):
        county_id = s * COUNTIES_PER_STATE + c
        alpha_i = state_level[s] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.7)   # county permanent level
        for t in YEARS:
            # Named controls (applicant composition), drawn per county-year.
            income = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0)                 # standardized log applicant income
            ltv    = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0)                 # standardized loan-to-value
            post_treat = 1 if (not np.isnan(G) and t >= G) else 0
            gap = (alpha_i
                   + year_shock[t]
                   + TAU_TRUE * post_treat
                   + GAMMA_INCOME * income
                   + GAMMA_LTV * ltv
                   + rng.normal(0.0, SIGMA))
            rows.append({
                "county":  county_id,
                "state":   s,
                "year":    t,
                "cohort_G": G,                 # year the state's program took effect (NaN = never)
                "post_treat": post_treat,      # 1 once this county's state has an active program
                "income":  income,
                "ltv":     ltv,
                "gap":     gap,                # OUTCOME: minority-white denial gap, pp
            })

panel = pd.DataFrame(rows)
panel["adopter"] = panel["cohort_G"].notna().astype(int)

print(f"county-year rows : {len(panel):,}")
print(f"states (clusters): {panel['state'].nunique()}")
print(f"counties         : {panel['county'].nunique()}")
print(f"adopting states  : {panel.loc[panel['adopter']==1, 'state'].nunique()}"
      f"   never-adopters: {panel.loc[panel['adopter']==0, 'state'].nunique()}")
print(f"PLANTED true ATT : {TAU_TRUE:+.2f} pp  (kept hidden from the spec; used only to grade it)")
panel.head()
A quick, non-confirmatory sanity look at the schema — the kind of glance at structure that does not touch any coefficient. We confirm the panel is balanced and that the treatment switches on at the right cohort years. Looking at the design (who is treated, when) is always allowed; looking at the outcome’s relationship to treatment before the gate is exactly what the freeze forbids.
# Balance + treatment-timing check (design only -- no outcome regression here).
counts = panel.groupby("year").size()
print("rows per year (should be constant -> balanced panel):")
print(counts.to_string())

print("\ntreated county-year cells by cohort:")
timing = (panel[panel["adopter"] == 1]
          .groupby("cohort_G")["post_treat"].agg(["mean", "size"])
          .rename(columns={"mean": "share_post", "size": "county_years"}))
print(timing.to_string())

assert panel.groupby(["county", "year"]).size().max() == 1, "panel must be one row per county-year"
print("\nSchema OK: balanced county-year panel, staggered adoption, never-adopter controls present.")

The PAP-FILED gate — frozen until the plan is a tagged commit> ## PAP-FILED GATE>> The primary specification below does not run until the pre-analysis plan is filed.>> In Lab 7 the PAP and the identification memo are committed and tagged (git tag pap-filed). You flip it to True only once the plan is genuinely filed —> and once it is filed, you may not change the spec to chase a nicer number.This is the freeze made mechanical. # Flip to True ONLY after the PAP + identification memo are filed as a tagged commit (Lab 7).
# Setting it True here represents Maya having filed `git tag pap-filed`.
PAP_FILED = True

# The pre-registered primary spec, frozen in advance, transcribed verbatim from the PAP's section 4.
# Changing any field after filing would break the contract (and would be logged as a deviation).
PRIMARY_SPEC = {
    "outcome":    "gap",                 # county-year minority-white denial gap (pp)
    "treatment":  "post_treat",          # 1 once the county's state has an active exam program
    "controls":   ["income", "ltv"],     # applicant-composition covariates (named in the PAP)
    "fixed_effects": ["county", "year"], # county and year FE
    "cluster":    "state",               # CLUSTER at the level treatment varies -- chosen in advance
    "test":       "two-sided",           # H1 effect direction is negative; report two-sided to be strict
}

print("PAP_FILED =", PAP_FILED)
for k, v in PRIMARY_SPEC.items():
    print(f"  {k:14s}: {v}")

title: nb7.5 — First-Look Regressions: Frozen Until the PAP Is Filed
section: 3. Run the pre-registered primary specification — once
text:
3. Run the pre-registered primary specification — once
Here is the spec, in CONVENTIONS §4 form, exactly as the PAP’s §4 line states it:

Outcome: gap (county-year minority–white denial gap, pp). Treatment / key regressor: post_treat (= 1 once the county’s state has an active fair-lending examination program). Controls: income, ltv (applicant-composition covariates). Fixed effects: county and year. Clustering: by state (the level at which treatment varies). Sample: the full balanced county-year panel, 2014–2023. Identifying assumption (one sentence): absent the examination programs, adopting and never-adopting states’ county-level denial gaps would have moved in parallel.

In pyfixest syntax that is one line: feols("gap ~ post_treat + income + ltv | county + year", ...) with the standard errors pre-specified as clustered by state via vcov={"CRV1": "state"}. The clustering choice is not a knob we turn after seeing the t-stat — Chapter 7.3 called that “p-hacking on the standard error.” It was nailed down in the PAP, so we read off whatever it gives.
The analysis cell asserts PAP_FILED before doing anything. If the plan were not filed, the cell would raise and refuse to estimate.

# ---- THE GATE: refuse to estimate until the PAP is filed --------------------
assert PAP_FILED, (
    "PAP NOT FILED. The primary specification is frozen until the pre-analysis plan and "
    "identification memo are committed and tagged (git tag pap-filed). Flip PAP_FILED to True "
    "ONLY after filing -- and do not change the spec to chase a result."
)

# ---- Build the formula straight from the frozen PRIMARY_SPEC (no hand-editing) ----
rhs_controls = " + ".join(PRIMARY_SPEC["controls"])
fe           = " + ".join(PRIMARY_SPEC["fixed_effects"])
formula = f'{PRIMARY_SPEC["outcome"]} ~ {PRIMARY_SPEC["treatment"]} + {rhs_controls} | {fe}'
print("Estimating (verbatim from PAP S4):")
print("   ", formula)
print("    SEs: clustered by", PRIMARY_SPEC["cluster"], "(pre-specified)\n")

# ---- Run it ONCE, with the PRE-SPECIFIED clustered standard errors -------------
primary = pf.feols(formula, data=panel, vcov={"CRV1": PRIMARY_SPEC["cluster"]})

print(primary.tidy().round(4).to_string())

section: 4. Report the headline number — with the pre-specified clustered SEs
text:
4. Report the headline number — with the pre-specified clustered SEs
Pull the one coefficient H1 is about — the coefficient on post_treat — together with its clustered standard error, t-statistic, p-value, and 95% confidence interval. This is the headline number the identification memo defends, reported exactly as promised. Because we built the world, we can also check the honest run against the planted truth: the confidence interval should comfortably cover \tau.

key = PRIMARY_SPEC["treatment"]

beta = float(primary.coef()[key])
se   = float(primary.se()[key])
tval = float(primary.tstat()[key])
pval = float(primary.pvalue()[key])
ci   = primary.confint().loc[key]
lo, hi = float(ci.iloc[0]), float(ci.iloc[1])

print("=" * 60)
print("  PRIMARY SPECIFICATION -- CONFIRMATORY RESULT (H1)")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"  coefficient on {key:<12s}: {beta:+.4f} pp")
print(f"  clustered SE (by state)   : {se:.4f}")
print(f"  t-statistic               : {tval:+.3f}")
print(f"  p-value (two-sided)       : {pval:.4g}")
print(f"  95% CI (clustered)        : [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]")
print("-" * 60)
print(f"  planted true ATT          : {TAU_TRUE:+.4f} pp")
covered = lo <= TAU_TRUE <= hi
print(f"  CI covers the truth?      : {covered}")
print("=" * 60)

# Honest-machinery checks: the pre-registered spec, run once, recovers the planted effect.
assert covered, "clustered 95% CI failed to cover the planted ATT -- spec is not recovering the truth"
assert beta < 0, "expected a NEGATIVE effect (programs narrow the gap); sign is wrong"
assert abs(beta - TAU_TRUE) < 0.30, "point estimate drifted too far from the planted truth"
print("\nRecovered: the frozen primary spec lands on the planted effect, with clustered SEs.")

A coefficient plot of the single confirmatory estimate — point estimate and clustered 95% interval — against the planted truth. One number, reported once. The plot is the whole confirmatory result; there is nothing else on this canvas, because there is nothing else in the primary analysis.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.2))
ax.errorbar([beta], [0], xerr=[[beta - lo], [hi - beta]],
            fmt="o", color="#3b6ea5", capsize=6, markersize=9,
            label="primary estimate (clustered 95% CI)")
ax.axvline(TAU_TRUE, color="green", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"planted truth ({TAU_TRUE:+.2f})")
ax.axvline(0.0, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1, label="no effect")
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("effect on minority-white denial gap (pp)")
ax.set_title("nb7.5 -- the ONE confirmatory number (primary spec, clustered SEs)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("nb75_primary_coef.png", dpi=110)
plt.close(fig)
print("saved figure: nb75_primary_coef.png")
print("That single estimate -- and only that estimate -- is the confirmatory result of the project.")

—## The confirmatory analysis is now COMPLETE.The headline number above is the entire pre-registered result. Everything below this line isEXPLORATORY — generated after seeing the data, valuable as a source of new hypotheses, but not aconfirmatory test of this project’s H1. It is fenced off and labeled so it can never be mistaken forthe registered result. This is the confirmatory/exploratory partition of Chapter 7.3.1, drawn on thepage where a reader can see exactly which results were tests and which were searches.—## 5. EXPLORATORY — not confirmatory> EXPLORATORY ZONE. Nothing below was pre-registered. These are post-hoc looks: they generate> hypotheses for the next study, they do not test this one. Reporting any of them as if it were the> primary result would be exactly the laundering of exploration as confirmation that the PAP exists to> prevent.To make the danger concrete, we walk a few forks Maya might be tempted by after seeing her headline —the same “garden of forking paths” from Chapter 7.3.1. Each is a perfectly defensible choice inisolation; each is a different number; and choosing among them by which gives the prettiest star isp-hacking. We run them only to show the forks, all clearly stamped exploratory.

# EXPLORATORY: a handful of alternative specifications Maya did NOT pre-register.
# Shown to illustrate the garden of forking paths -- NOT to be reported as the result.
explore = {}

# Fork A: drop the controls.
explore["no controls"] = pf.feols("gap ~ post_treat | county + year",
                                  data=panel, vcov={"CRV1": "state"})
# Fork B: cluster by county instead of state (a DIFFERENT, non-registered SE choice).
explore["cluster by county"] = pf.feols(
    "gap ~ post_treat + income + ltv | county + year",
    data=panel, vcov={"CRV1": "county"})
# Fork C: drop 2020 (a post-hoc sample exclusion).
explore["drop 2020"] = pf.feols(
    "gap ~ post_treat + income + ltv | county + year",
    data=panel[panel["year"] != 2020].copy(), vcov={"CRV1": "state"})
# Fork D: add a control on the causal pathway (over-controlling -- a tempting but wrong fork).
panel_x = panel.copy()
panel_x["loan_size"] = 0.5 * panel_x["ltv"] + 0.4 * panel_x["post_treat"] + rng.normal(0, 1, len(panel_x))
explore["over-control (bad)"] = pf.feols(
    "gap ~ post_treat + income + ltv + loan_size | county + year",
    data=panel_x, vcov={"CRV1": "state"})

forks = pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        "beta": float(m.coef()["post_treat"]),
        "se":   float(m.se()["post_treat"]),
        "pval": float(m.pvalue()["post_treat"]),
    } for name, m in explore.items()
}).T
# Put the registered result at the top for contrast.
forks.loc["** PRIMARY (registered) **"] = [beta, se, pval]
forks = forks.reindex(["** PRIMARY (registered) **"] + list(explore.keys()))

print("EXPLORATORY forks vs. the one registered spec (all clearly labeled):\n")
print(forks.round(4).to_string())
print("\nEvery row is a defensible choice in isolation; only the top row is the confirmatory test.")
print("Picking a row by which gives the smallest p-value is the garden of forking paths (Ch 7.3.1).")

Plot the forks side by side against the planted truth. They scatter — that scatter is the researcher degrees of freedom Chapter 7.3 warned about. Note especially the over-control fork: by conditioning on a variable that sits on the treatment’s causal pathway, it absorbs part of the very effect we are hunting and biases the estimate toward zero (the Mentor 4 over-controlling trap). The point of showing it is not to choose among these; it is to make visible why the choice had to be frozen before this picture existed.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ypos = np.arange(len(forks))[::-1]
colors = ["#b5651d" if "PRIMARY" not in name else "#3b6ea5" for name in forks.index]
ax.errorbar(forks["beta"], ypos, xerr=1.96 * forks["se"],
            fmt="o", capsize=5, markersize=8, ecolor="grey", linestyle="none",
            mfc="none")
for y, (name, row), col in zip(ypos, forks.iterrows(), colors):
    ax.plot(row["beta"], y, "o", color=col, markersize=9)
ax.axvline(TAU_TRUE, color="green", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"planted truth ({TAU_TRUE:+.2f})")
ax.axvline(0.0, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(ypos)
ax.set_yticklabels(forks.index, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("effect on denial gap (pp), 95% CI")
ax.set_title("EXPLORATORY: the garden of forking paths (blue = registered; orange = post-hoc)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("nb75_forks.png", dpi=110)
plt.close(fig)
print("saved figure: nb75_forks.png")

section: 6. Proving the gate works
text:
6. Proving the gate works
Before we leave the discipline, let us show the gate has teeth. If PAP_FILED were False, the analysis cell’s assert would fire and refuse to estimate. We demonstrate it here in a contained way — catching the error so the notebook still runs end-to-end — so you can see the freeze is real and not decorative.

def run_primary(pap_filed_flag):
    """The gated analysis, factored out so we can demonstrate the freeze both ways."""
    assert pap_filed_flag, (
        "PAP NOT FILED -- primary specification is frozen until `git tag pap-filed`."
    )
    return pf.feols(formula, data=panel, vcov={"CRV1": PRIMARY_SPEC["cluster"]})

# With the PAP NOT filed, the gate must block the run:
try:
    run_primary(pap_filed_flag=False)
    print("UNEXPECTED: the gate did not fire.")
except AssertionError as e:
    print("GATE FIRED (as it should) when PAP_FILED is False:")
    print("   ", str(e))

# With the PAP filed, it runs and reproduces the same headline coefficient:
m_again = run_primary(pap_filed_flag=True)
print(f"\nGate open (PAP filed) -> coefficient reproduces: {float(m_again.coef()['post_treat']):+.4f} pp")
assert abs(float(m_again.coef()["post_treat"]) - beta) < 1e-9, "gated run must match the headline exactly"
print("The freeze is mechanical: no plan, no regression.")

section: 7. The bridge to Week 8 — robustness comes next, on the frozen result
text:
7. The bridge to Week 8 — robustness comes next, on the frozen result
You now have your headline number, and you have it honestly: one pre-registered specification, run once, with the standard errors you chose in advance. What you do not do is start swapping specifications to see which looks best — that was the whole point of the freeze.
So what do you do next? Week 8 is robustness, run on this frozen result. The threats-and-responses table you built in the identification memo (Ch 7.5) becomes the skeleton of your robustness section: Chapter 8.2 is, almost literally, the instruction “go run column 3 for every row of your table” — the placebo tests, the alternative standard errors, the sample and bandwidth perturbations you promised in your PAP’s §5 to report whichever way they come out. The exploratory forks in Section 5 above are not that: they are unregistered searches, useful only for generating next-study hypotheses. A planned robustness check is a fork you committed to walking in advance and to reporting honestly; that is what makes it confirmatory-grade rather than fishing.
The thread of the whole week, one last time: the PAP says you did not fish, and the identification memo says the pond is the right pond. This notebook ran the first cast — once, under the freeze. Week 8 is where you stress-test the fish you caught, on the result you are no longer allowed to change.


Your Turn

Move the truth. Change TAU_TRUE to 0.0 (a true null) and re-run. The primary spec should now produce a confidence interval that covers zero — the pre-registered honest null Chapter 7.3.4 said is a genuine contribution, not a failure. Notice you did not get to go fishing for a star.
Strain the clusters. In adopt_cohort, make only 2 or 3 states ever adopt. Re-run the primary spec. Watch the clustered standard error balloon — with few treated clusters, cluster-robust inference is strained (Ch 4.1’s few-treated-clusters warning). What would your PAP’s §5 placebo permutation say here, and why is it the more honest summary?
Audit a fork. Pick one EXPLORATORY fork from Section 5 whose number you liked better than the registered one. Write the single sentence you would have to put in a deviation log (Ch 7.3.3) to use it instead — including the honest clause: was the change prompted by seeing the coefficient? If yes, it is exploratory, full stop.

title: Week 8 — Independent Research Project II: Execution, Robustness, Poster, and Defense
text:
Ch 8.1 — Execution & Specification Curve (confirmatory run; multiverse analysis; deviations log)

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
text:
8.1.1 The confirmatory run: execute exactly what you filed, report whatever it shows
Maya filed her pre-analysis plan two weeks ago. It sits in her repository as a tagged commit, pap-filed, time-stamped and frozen, with one primary specification written out in full spec-discipline form and a deviation log waiting empty beside it. The hard thinking is done. What remains, this week, is the part that feels like it should be easy: run the thing. Open the notebook, point it at the confirmation data, execute the one regression she promised, and read the number off the table.
It is easy. It is also where most honest projects quietly go wrong, because the moment a result appears on the screen, the discipline of Week 7 stops being a document and starts being a test of character. The PAP told Maya which regression to run. It did not, and could not, run it for her — and it cannot stop her from running thirty more once she has seen the first. This chapter is about that moment. It teaches you to execute the pre-registered confirmatory result exactly as filed and report it whatever it shows; then to take the garden of forking paths you wrote down in Chapter 7.3 and make it visible — to run not one specification but every defensible one, plot the whole distribution of estimates, and read off whether your headline is a robust feature of the data or a lucky branch in a forest of paths. The instrument that does this is the specification curve, and it is the single most honest picture you can put in an empirical paper.
We follow the book’s reveal-the-trick structure. State what the confirmatory run is and run it; state what the garden of forking paths costs you and make it visible with a multiverse of specifications; learn to read the resulting curve honestly — fragile or robust?; and see when the curve itself lies. The intellectual frame is Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson’s specification-curve analysis.
A boundary first, so you do not go looking for the wrong thing here. This chapter is about analytic-choice multiplicity — the fact that one dataset and one hypothesis admit many defensible regressions, and that the choice among them is a hidden multiple-testing problem. The next chapter, 8.2, is about inference validity — whether the one design you chose actually identifies what you claim, stress-tested with placebos and Oster’s \delta. They are different anxieties. The spec curve asks “does my result survive the choices I could defensibly have made differently?” The robustness tests of 8.2 ask “is the design I committed to even the right design?” Do not conflate them; this week pulls them apart on purpose.
Here is the result in one sentence: your first job in Week 8 is to run the pre-registered primary specification once, on the confirmation data, exactly as written in the PAP — no edits, no peeking-then-tweaking — and to report the number it produces no matter which way it falls.
That sounds trivial. It is the hardest professional habit in the entire course, and the reason is psychological, not technical. Go back to Chapter 1.5 and the logic of what a p-value means. You proved there that under a true null the p-value is uniformly distributed on [0,1], so a single pre-specified test at \alpha=0.05 rejects a true null exactly 5% of the time — that 5% is the contract you signed. The contract only holds if the test was fixed before you saw the outcome. The instant you run a regression, look at the coefficient, dislike it, and adjust the specification to improve it, you have re-entered the garden of forking paths of Chapter 7.3, and your p-value no longer means 5%. It means something larger and unknowable, inflated by every fork you walked with the answer in view. The PAP froze the forks. The confirmatory run is the act of honoring that freeze.
So the mechanics are deliberately rigid. Maya’s pap-filed commit named, in CONVENTIONS §4 form, a single staggered difference-in-differences: outcome the county-year minority–white denial gap; treatment a state’s active fair-lending examination program; never-adopters and not-yet-treated states as clean controls; county and year fixed effects; standard errors clustered by state; the sample pinned to a fixed HMDA vintage. Her notebook, notebooks/week-07/nb7.5-first-look-regressions.ipynb, is frozen behind a gate — a flag PAP_FILED=True that must be asserted before the analysis cell will run, the technological enforcement of “do not peek until the plan is filed.” When she ran it, exactly once, the pre-registered estimator returned
\widehat{\text{ATT}} = -1.89 \text{ percentage points}, \qquad \text{SE}_{\text{clustered by state}} = 0.065, \qquad 95\%\ \text{CI} = [-2.02,\ -1.75].
The examination programs are associated with a roughly 1.9-percentage-point narrowing of the denial gap, the sign she hypothesized, with a confidence interval comfortably away from zero. That is the confirmatory result. It is the number the rest of the paper defends, and it is the number she reports in her headline table — full stop, with the clustering flavor labeled and the CI shown.
Now the part that separates a researcher from a result-shopper. Maya must commit, in advance, to reporting that number whichever way it came out. Suppose the confirmatory run had returned \widehat{\text{ATT}} = -0.3 pp with a CI of [-1.9,\ +1.3] — a wide interval straddling zero. Her PAP’s falsification clause already told her what to do: a wide CI that includes zero is a power failure, reported as inconclusive, not as a refutation; a tight CI hugging zero would be a genuine, publishable null about fair-lending policy. Either way she reports it. The temptation — and it is enormous, because she has spent five weeks on this and wants the effect to be real — is to treat a disappointing confirmatory number as a problem to be debugged rather than a result to be reported. That instinct is the disease. The whole architecture of Week 7 exists to make the confirmatory number binding: you wrote down what it would mean before you knew what it would be, precisely so that knowing what it is cannot change what it means.
There is a subtle trap even inside an honest confirmatory run, and it is worth naming because beginners fall into it constantly. The trap is mistaking a clean execution for a robust result. Maya ran exactly one specification and got a starred coefficient. That is necessary but not sufficient for a credible finding, because the one specification she ran was one branch of a tree she could defensibly have climbed differently. Her PAP committed her to clustering by state — but clustering by county was also defensible. It committed her to county and year fixed effects — but adding state-specific linear trends was also defensible. It committed her to a particular sample window — but trimming the COVID-disrupted year 2020 was also defensible. Each of those alternatives is a fork she chose not to walk, and a reader is entitled to ask: if you had walked them, would the -1.9 still be there, or would it dissolve? The confirmatory run answers “what does the pre-registered specification say?” It does not answer “is the answer an artifact of that one specification?” For that, you need to make the whole garden visible. That is the rest of this chapter.

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: 8.1.2 The garden of forking paths, made visible
text:
8.1.2 The garden of forking paths, made visible
You met the garden of forking paths in Chapter 7.3 as a threat: the reason an honest researcher can p-hack without a single dishonest thought, by making a sequence of reasonable, outcome-aware choices that each nudge the coefficient the desired way. The PAP’s defense was to nail down the forks in advance so they collapse to one confirmatory test. That defense protects your headline. But it leaves a question hanging that the PAP cannot answer, because the PAP is a single path through the garden: how many of the other defensible paths would have given you the same answer?
The specification curve, due to Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson (2020), answers exactly that question by refusing to hide. Their insight is to invert the usual sin. The p-hacker runs many specifications and reports the one that looks best, hiding the rest. The specification-curve analyst runs many specifications — ideally all the defensible ones — and reports all of them at once, as a distribution. Where p-hacking exploits multiplicity by concealment, specification-curve analysis defangs multiplicity by exhaustive disclosure. If your result is a robust feature of the data, it will be there across most of the forest; if it is a lucky branch, the picture will say so loudly, and you will have caught yourself before a referee does.
The procedure has three steps, and the discipline is entirely in the first one.
Step 1 — Enumerate the defensible analytic choices. This is the act of writing the garden down. You list, for each decision in your analysis, every option a reasonable, competent researcher could have chosen — and, crucially, only the defensible ones. The point is not to include absurd specifications to pad the count; a specification you would never defend in a seminar does not belong in the multiverse, because including it would let you smuggle in noise and then hide behind “but the median was fine.” The choices for Maya’s HMDA DiD partition naturally into the seven slots of CONVENTIONS §4:

Controls. Which county-year applicant-composition covariates enter? She could include the income distribution, the loan-to-value distribution, the loan-amount distribution — or any subset. Reasonable researchers disagree about how many composition controls a doubly-robust DiD needs. Call this 4 defensible combinations (none, income only, income+LTV, all three).
Fixed effects. County and year FE are the baseline. Does she also add state-specific linear time trends (a common parallel-trends hedge)? With or without: 2 options.
Sample window. Full period; drop 2020 (COVID); drop the first and last adoption cohorts (thinly identified): 3 options.
Clustering / inference. Cluster by state (her pre-registered choice); cluster by county; wild-cluster bootstrap by state (defensible when adopting states are few, per Chapter 4.1): 3 options.
Outcome definition. The denial gap (minority denial rate minus white denial rate); or two separate outcomes — the minority denial level and a within-applicant denial indicator; the gap measured as a difference vs. a log-ratio: say 2 defensible outcome operationalizations.

Multiply them: 4 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2 = 144 specifications. Each is a single point in what the multiverse literature calls the garden of forking paths made into a grid — every combination of every defensible choice, laid out so none can hide. Notice that one of those 144 is her pre-registered primary specification. The confirmatory run is not outside the multiverse; it is a labeled, privileged point inside it.
Here the arithmetic of Week 1 comes back to bite, and it is the reason this whole exercise matters. Recall from Chapter 1.5 that if you test 20 independent true nulls at \alpha=0.05, the chance at least one crosses the line by luck is 1-(1-0.05)^{20}\approx 0.64 — a coin-flip-beating probability of a spurious “winner” purely from giving luck enough tries. With 144 specifications, even if the true effect were exactly zero, the probability that at least one lands at p<0.05 is overwhelming. The garden of forking paths is just multiple testing wearing the disguise of “I only ran one regression.” Maya did only run one regression for the confirmatory result — but the 144 specifications measure how many regressions she could defensibly have run, which is the real size of her multiple-testing problem. The specification curve does not eliminate that problem. It does something better: it shows you the whole distribution of what luck and choice together could produce, so a single starred specification can never again masquerade as the only one you ever considered.
Step 2 — Run all of them. Estimate the key coefficient — for Maya, the ATT on the denial gap — under every one of the 144 specifications, and collect the estimates and their confidence intervals into a table. This is mechanical and embarrassingly fast on modern hardware; 144 fixed-effects regressions on a county-year panel run in seconds. The output is a vector of 144 estimates and 144 inference results, plus, for each one, a record of which choice was made in each slot. That record is the load-bearing part, as Step 3 reveals.
Step 3 — Plot the distribution, with the choices underneath. The specification curve is a two-panel figure that has become the signature of this method, and once you have read one you cannot unsee it. We build it next.

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: 8.1.3 Reading the specification curve
text:
8.1.3 Reading the specification curve
The figure has two stacked panels that share a horizontal axis. The horizontal axis runs over all 144 specifications, sorted by the magnitude of the estimate — most negative on the left, most positive on the right.
The top panel plots the 144 point estimates as a curve (hence the name), each with a marker for its confidence interval — colored or filled when the specification is statistically significant at your chosen level, hollow when it is not. Because the specifications are sorted by estimate, the curve rises monotonically from left to right; its shape is the whole story. A flat curve sitting entirely below zero, with nearly every marker filled, says: every defensible path gives roughly the same negative answer, and almost all are significant. A curve that sweeps from strongly negative through zero up to strongly positive, with a mix of filled and hollow markers, says: the sign and significance of my result depend entirely on which fork I walk — a result that is an artifact of analytic choice, not a feature of the world.
The bottom panel is the part that turns a pretty picture into a diagnostic. It is a grid: one row per analytic choice (cluster-by-state, cluster-by-county, drop-2020, add-state-trends, income-control-only, …), and one column per specification, aligned to the top panel’s sort order. A tick mark sits at (\text{row}, \text{column}) when that specification used that choice. So you read downward from any interesting region of the curve to see exactly which choices produced it. If all the positive, insignificant specifications on the right share a single tick — say, every one of them used “cluster by county” plus “drop 2020” — then you have learned something precise and damning: the result’s fragility is driven by those two choices. The bottom panel converts “my result is fragile” from a vague worry into a forensic finding: this specific fork is the one that flips my sign.
Let us read Maya’s curve concretely, because the reading is the skill. Suppose her 144 specifications produce a curve like this: the estimates run from about -2.4 pp on the left to about -0.4 pp on the right; the median is around -1.8 pp; about 132 of the 144 are significant at the 5% level (filled), and the dozen hollow ones cluster at the right end near zero. Reading downward from those dozen non-significant specifications, the bottom panel shows they all share two choices: the wild-cluster bootstrap (which widens intervals when adopters are few) combined with the “drop first and last cohorts” sample (which throws away identifying variation). That is an honest, interpretable picture, and here is exactly what Maya should write about it:

Across all 144 defensible specifications, the estimated effect of fair-lending examinations on the minority–white denial gap is negative, with a median of -1.8 pp and a range of [-2.4, -0.4] pp. The pre-registered primary specification (-1.9 pp) sits near the center of this distribution. The effect is statistically significant in 132 of 144 specifications (92%); the twelve exceptions combine the wild-cluster bootstrap with the most aggressive sample trim, which jointly maximize the standard error while minimizing identifying variation — i.e., the result loses significance only in the lowest-power corner of the multiverse, and never changes sign.

That is a robust result, and the curve is what licenses the word. The sign never flips; the magnitude is stable around the pre-registered estimate; loss of significance is confined to specifications that are independently the least powerful, for reasons the bottom panel makes legible. A referee reading that paragraph and that figure cannot accuse Maya of cherry-picking, because she has shown them the entire orchard and pointed to exactly which trees bear less fruit and why.
Now contrast the picture that should terrify you, and would have, had Sam built a specification curve for his momentum anomaly. Sam’s project from Week 7 asks whether past-12-month winners outperform losers next month — a portfolio sort with a long menu of defensible forks: the formation window (12 months, or 12 skipping the most recent, or 6); the holding period (1 month, 3, 6); value- versus equal-weighting; NYSE breakpoints versus all-stock breakpoints; including or excluding microcaps and penny stocks; the sample period (full history, or post-2000, or excluding 2008–09). Those forks easily multiply past 200 specifications. Suppose Sam’s curve sweeps from a significantly negative long-short return on the left, through a fat band of insignificant near-zero estimates in the middle, up to a significantly positive return on the right — and the bottom panel reveals that every significantly positive specification shares one choice: “include microcaps, equal-weighted.” Reading downward tells the whole story in one glance: the anomaly is not a feature of the cross-section of returns; it is a feature of how you weight tiny, illiquid, hard-to-trade stocks. The headline “momentum earns 80 bps a month” was a single branch — the equal-weighted-microcap branch — and the curve drags it into the light. Sam’s honest sentence is the mirror image of Maya’s: the sign of the momentum premium is not robust to the weighting and universe choices; it is positive and significant only under equal-weighting with microcaps included, and is statistically indistinguishable from zero under the value-weighted, liquid-universe specifications that a tradable strategy would actually face. That sentence kills the easy paper and replaces it with a true and far more interesting one.
The general reading rule, then, is a short checklist you apply to every specification curve you build or referee:

Where does the sign live? If estimates span both signs, your effect’s direction is choice-dependent — the most serious possible fragility. If they all share a sign, the direction is robust even if the magnitude wanders.
Where does the pre-registered specification sit? Mark it on the curve. If your confirmatory estimate sits near the center of the distribution, your headline is representative. If it sits at an extreme tail, you must explain why — and “I happened to pre-register the best-looking corner” is not a flattering explanation, even when innocent.
What fraction is significant, and where do the exceptions cluster? Read the hollow markers downward into the bottom panel. Significance lost in the low-power corner (small samples, conservative inference) is benign; significance that appears only under one or two specific choices is a red flag pointing straight at those choices.
Which rows of the bottom panel drive the spread? The choice whose ticks best separate the left of the curve from the right is the fork your result is most sensitive to. Name it. It is the thing a skeptic will attack, and the thing your robustness section (8.2) must address head-on.

A word on the formal inference that Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson attach to the curve, kept light because the picture is most of the value. They propose a permutation test on the whole curve: under the sharp null that the effect is zero everywhere, you re-shuffle the treatment assignment, recompute all 144 specifications on each shuffle, and ask whether the observed curve — for instance, the number of significant-and-correctly-signed specifications, or the median estimate — is more extreme than what the null curves produce. This tests the multiverse as a whole rather than any single specification, which is precisely the right unit of analysis once you admit that “which specification” was itself a choice. For a high-school capstone, computing the descriptive curve and reading it with the checklist above is the required deliverable; the permutation test is an extension in nb8.1 for those who want the formal p-value on the entire forest. [CHECK: confirm the exact page within Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson (2020) where the joint permutation-inference procedure is stated, for a pinpoint cite.]

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: 8.1.4 When the specification curve lies
text:
8.1.4 When the specification curve lies
Reveal-the-trick demands the third move: every technique has an assumption that breaks, and a picture this persuasive is dangerous precisely because it is persuasive. A specification curve can mislead in four distinct ways, and an honest analyst flags which ones apply.
The curve only contains the forks you chose to enumerate. This is the deepest limitation and the easiest to forget once the beautiful figure is on the page. A specification curve is exhaustive over the choices you listed and silent about every choice you did not think to vary. If Maya’s entire multiverse holds the outcome definition nearly fixed — if all 144 specifications quietly assume the denial gap is the right outcome and never test the within-applicant denial indicator — then her curve can look gloriously robust while resting on one unexamined fork. The curve’s robustness is conditional on the completeness of the enumeration, and completeness is a judgment call, not a guarantee. The defense is to enumerate the forks honestly and broadly, and to state in the paper which dimensions you held fixed and why — exactly the spec-discipline of CONVENTIONS §4, now applied to the meta-decision of what to vary.
Not all specifications are equally defensible, and the curve pretends they are. A naive reading treats all 144 points as equal votes, so that “the median is negative” sounds like a democratic verdict. But some of those specifications are better than others — clustering at the level treatment varies (state) is more defensible than clustering by county; a doubly-robust DiD with composition controls is better-identified than one without. If you pad the multiverse with weak-but-arguable specifications, you can drag the median wherever you like, which is p-hacking with extra steps and a fancier chart. Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson are explicit that the choices must be theoretically justified and statistically valid — not merely “things you could type into the regression.” The honest move is to include only specifications you would defend out loud, and, where they genuinely differ in quality, to say so rather than hide behind the median.
The curve describes analytic-choice fragility, not identification. A specification curve can be flat, tight, all-significant, and completely wrong, because every one of its 144 specifications can share the same fatal identification flaw. If Maya’s parallel-trends assumption fails — if adopting states were already on a different denial-gap trajectory — then all 144 specifications inherit that bias, and the curve will robustly report a beautifully stable artifact. Robustness across the multiverse is not the same as validity of the design. This is the boundary from this chapter’s opening, restated as a warning: the spec curve answers “did my choices drive the result?” and is mute on “did my design identify the effect?” The second question is Chapter 8.2’s job, with the placebos and Oster-\delta stress tests that probe the assumption itself. A robust spec curve on an invalid design is a confident wrong answer — the most expensive kind.
The curve can become a fishing license if you let it. There is a perverse failure mode where a researcher runs the multiverse, then picks the specification at the center of the distribution and reports that as the headline — “I chose the median specification, the most representative one.” But the median was determined by the data you have already seen, so choosing it after the fact is just outcome-driven specification selection in a lab coat. The discipline that prevents this is the one you already have: the PAP fixes the primary specification in advance, and the spec curve is reported around that pre-registered point, not used to choose it. The confirmatory run comes first and is privileged; the curve is context for it, never a substitute. This is why the order in this chapter is not negotiable — confirmatory result in §8.1.1, multiverse in §8.1.2 — and why the curve always marks where the pre-registered specification sits.
The summary is the one Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson themselves press: a specification curve is a tool for honesty about analytic-choice multiplicity, and it is extraordinarily good at that one job. It is not a robustness panacea, not a substitute for a credible identifying assumption, and not a way to launder a post-hoc choice into a pre-registered one. Use it for what it is — the most complete possible disclosure of the garden of forking paths — and say plainly what it does not do.

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: 8.1.5 The honest deviations log
text:
8.1.5 The honest deviations log
You filed a PAP. You ran the confirmatory specification. You built the spec curve. Somewhere in that process — it is nearly inevitable, as Chapter 7.3 warned via Olken’s perils — reality forced you off the plan. A control you swore you would include turned out to be collinear with a fixed effect and dropped out. A clustering variable was corrupted for 4% of rows. The COVID year behaved so strangely you had to handle it differently than you guessed. The deviations log is the running, dated record of every departure from the PAP — what changed, why, and, the crucial part, whether the change was prompted by seeing the outcome.
Deviating is not the sin; Week 7 said this and it bears repeating now that you are actually doing the analysis and the temptation is live rather than hypothetical. Hiding the deviation is the sin, and outcome-driven deviation is the specific sin the whole apparatus exists to catch. So every entry in the log carries a verdict on one binary question: was this change forced on me by a mechanical reality, or did I make it because I saw the coefficient and did not like it?

A deviation forced by a mechanical reality — collinearity, a coding bug, a data-availability surprise, a cluster identifier that was corrupted — is innocent. You note it, you fix it, you move on. It is not outcome-driven; nothing about the result steered the change. Example entry: “PAP §2 specified clustering by state. On the confirmation data, the state identifier was missing for 4% of county-year cells due to a FIPS-merge gap. We clustered by the state-equivalent census region for those cells and re-ran; the ATT moved from -1.89 to -1.91 pp, immaterial. Not outcome-driven.”
A deviation prompted by seeing the outcome — you added a control after noticing it improved your t-stat, you trimmed a year after seeing it weakened the effect, you switched clustering because the pre-registered choice was insignificant — is exactly the garden of forking paths, and the log forces you to confront it as such. The honest response is not to pretend it didn’t happen but to report the result both ways and flag the deviating version as exploratory. Example entry: “After observing anomalous denial patterns in 2020, we added a year-2020 indicator interacted with treatment. This was prompted by the data, so it is outcome-driven. We report the pre-registered specification (no 2020 interaction) as the confirmatory result and the 2020-adjusted version as a labeled exploratory analysis, not as the headline.”

That last clause is the entire ethic of Week 8 in one move. The PAP is not a prison and the deviations log is not a confession booth; together they are the instrument that draws the line between confirmatory and exploratory honestly, in public, after the fact. A referee — or future-Maya, six months on — reads the deviations log and trusts the paper more, not less, because they can see exactly where the analysis was a test and where it became a search. The deepest point, carried straight from Olken in Chapter 7.3: the value of pre-registration is not that you never deviate, but that the reader can see where and why you did.
And the deviations log connects directly to the spec curve you just built, in a way that makes the two tools one system. Every deviation you were tempted to make for outcome-driven reasons — “should I have clustered by county instead? added that control? dropped that year?” — is already a fork in your multiverse. So when you are tempted, the disciplined response is not to silently switch the primary specification; it is to point at the spec curve and say: that alternative is specification number 87; here is where it sits; the headline does not depend on it. The spec curve is the honest home for every fork you were tempted to walk, and the deviations log is the honest record of the few you actually had to. Between them, there is no fork left in the dark.

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: 8.1.6 Where this goes next
text:
8.1.6 Where this goes next
You arrived at this chapter with a frozen plan and a frozen notebook. You leave it with three things on the page: a confirmatory result run exactly as pre-registered and reported whatever it showed; a specification curve that makes the entire garden of forking paths visible and tells you, with a forensic bottom panel, whether your headline is a robust feature of the data or a lucky branch; and an honest deviations log that draws the confirmatory/exploratory line in public. Together they are the answer to the question a skeptic asks first: would your result have been the same if you had made your defensible choices differently?
But notice what the spec curve cannot tell you, and what therefore comes next. Every specification in Maya’s robust, all-negative curve assumes parallel trends. If that assumption is false, the curve is a confident wrong answer. Chapter 8.2 turns from analytic-choice multiplicity to inference validity: the placebo tests that would have fired if the design were broken, and Oster’s \delta, which asks how much unobserved selection it would take to explain away your effect. The spec curve stress-tests your choices; 8.2 stress-tests your assumption. You need both before you defend the paper in 8.3 and hand it to a hostile peer reviewer in 8.4. A result that survives the multiverse and the placebos and the bound on omitted-variable bias is one you can present at the conference without flinching — because every honest attack has already been made, by you, first.

title: Chapter 8.1 — Execution & the Specification Curve
section: Your Turn
text:
Your Turn
Open nb8.1 — the specification-curve generator (notebooks/week-08/nb8.1-specification-curve.ipynb). It takes your project’s pre-registered primary specification — the one your pap-filed commit names and your nb7.5 first-look ran once — and builds the full multiverse around it. You will: (1) enumerate your defensible analytic choices slot by slot in CONVENTIONS §4 form (controls, fixed effects, sample window, clustering, outcome definition), and count the number of specifications the cross-product implies; (2) run every specification and collect the estimates, confidence intervals, and the choice-record for each; (3) draw the two-panel specification curve — estimates sorted on top, the choice grid aligned underneath — with your pre-registered specification marked; and (4) read it with the four-point checklist from §8.1.3, then write the one honest paragraph that describes your curve. The notebook ships Maya’s HMDA multiverse as the worked example (her curve sits robustly below zero, median \approx -1.8 pp) and Sam’s momentum multiverse as the cautionary one (sign flips with the weighting/universe choice). The optional extension implements the Simonsohn–Simmons–Nelson permutation test for a p-value on the whole forest.
Reflection prompts to carry into Lab 8 and the peer review.

Find the fork that flips your sign. Build your spec curve, then read the bottom panel: which single analytic choice, if any, best separates the significant specifications from the insignificant ones — or the negative estimates from the positive? Write the one sentence you will put in your paper naming that fork and stating honestly how much your headline depends on it. If no single fork drives the spread, say that, and explain why it is the stronger result.
Where does your pre-registered specification sit? Mark your confirmatory estimate on your own curve. Is it near the center (representative) or out in a tail? If it sits in a tail, write the honest explanation — and ask yourself whether, had you peeked first, you would have been tempted to pre-register exactly that corner. What in your Week-7 process prevented that?
Audit your deviations log against your multiverse. List every departure you made from your PAP on the confirmation data. For each, mark it mechanical or outcome-driven, and locate the corresponding specification in your spec curve. For any outcome-driven deviation, confirm that you reported the pre-registered version as the headline and the deviation as labeled-exploratory. If you cannot find a deviation’s alternative anywhere in your multiverse, your enumeration of forks was incomplete — go back and add it.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
text:
1. Alternative standard errors: is the t-statistic telling the truth?
In the last chapter you ran your pre-registered specification and then surrounded it with a specification curve — every defensible analytic choice, plotted, so a reader can see that your headline number is not an artifact of one lucky fork in the garden. That chapter was about analytic-choice multiplicity: the many regressions you could have run. This chapter is about something different and, frankly, more adversarial. Here you stop varying your choices and start attacking your inference itself. The question is no longer “is my estimate stable across reasonable specifications?” It is “is my estimate even real, or have I been fooled — by correlated errors that make my t-statistic lie, by a pattern that would show up even where no treatment happened, by a knob I tuned until the stars appeared, by a family of outcomes I tested all at once, or by a confounder I never measured?”
The discipline this chapter teaches has an ugly name and a beautiful purpose: you are going to try to kill your own result. Not soften it, not hedge it — kill it. You will design the tests a hostile referee would design, run them on yourself first, and report what they find whether or not you like the answer. This is the single most important professional habit in empirical work, and it is the one that separates a paper a reader trusts from one they merely read. The reveal-the-trick promise of this whole book gets turned, one last time, on you: the trick you are now revealing is the one you might be playing on yourself.
Here is the spine of the chapter, so you have it before the machinery. In Chapter 7.5 you wrote an identification memo with a threats-and-responses table — four columns, the third of which was “what we do about it.” Column 3 was a set of promises. This chapter is where those promises come due. Each robustness test below is the operationalization of one row’s column 3: a placebo for the “this pattern is spurious” threat, a wild cluster bootstrap for the “few clusters break my standard errors” threat, an Oster δ for the “unobserved confounder” threat. So as you read, keep your own threats table open. Every test here is an answer you owe to a row you already wrote.
We will continue with Maya’s project from Week 7: the staggered difference-in-differences on HMDA, asking whether state fair-lending examination programs reduced the county-level minority–white gap in mortgage-denial rates.1 Her identifying assumption is per-cohort parallel trends; her primary estimate is a Callaway–Sant’Anna overall ATT against never- and not-yet-treated controls (Chapter 4.2), clustered by state. Suppose she ran it and got an ATT of roughly −1.4 percentage points — the examination programs appear to shrink the denial gap by 1.4pp — with a state-clustered standard error of about 0.55, so a t of about 2.5 and three stars on the table. A good day. Now we spend the chapter trying to make that number die.
Start with the cheapest attack, because it is also the most common cause of a result that evaporates: the standard error is too small, so the t-statistic is too big, and the significance is an illusion. Recall the central lesson of Chapter 2.4: OLS gives you the right point estimate even when the errors misbehave; what misbehaving errors corrupt is the variance of that estimate — the standard error, hence the t-stat, hence the p-value. A robustness check on standard errors does not touch your \hat{\beta} at all. It re-asks the question “how uncertain is this number?” under a less convenient — and often more honest — set of assumptions about how the errors are correlated.
The sandwich estimator from Chapter 2.4 was the unifying object: \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\hat{\boldsymbol\Omega}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}, where the only thing that changes between SE flavors is what you assume about the error variance-covariance matrix \boldsymbol\Omega. Classical SEs assume \boldsymbol\Omega = \sigma^2\mathbf{I} — errors all the same size and uncorrelated. Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (HC1/HC2/HC3) let the diagonal of \boldsymbol\Omega vary. Cluster-robust SEs let \boldsymbol\Omega have correlated blocks. HAC (Newey–West) lets errors be correlated across time within a unit, with the correlation fading over a bandwidth. The robustness exercise is to re-run your headline estimate under each plausible flavor and watch the standard error move.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
text:
What it probes
Three distinct threats, all of which inflate your significance if you ignore them.
The clustering level. This is the one that bites Maya hardest, and the question is deceptively simple: at what level are the errors correlated? In Chapter 2.4 you learned the Petersen (2009) rule — cluster at the level of the correlation, and if treatment varies at the state level you must cluster at the state level, because the Moulton-style inflation factor 1+(n-1)\rho_x\rho_\varepsilon shows that within-state error correlation, combined with a treatment that is constant within state, can multiply the true variance many times over. The robustness check is to try the defensible alternatives and see if the verdict survives. Maya clusters by state in her primary spec. A referee might ask: what about clustering by county (her unit of observation)? Or two-way, by state and by year, since a national shock to mortgage markets in 2008 correlates errors across all states in that year (Cameron, Gelbach & Miller 2011)?2 The honest move is to report a small table:
