Read this top to bottom and you see the whole drama of Chapter 2.4 in one column. The classical SE is a fantasy — it treats every county-year as independent information and reports a t of 7.8 that no one should believe. As you move to coarser, more honest clustering, the SE roughly triples and the t falls from absurd to merely solid. The right reading: Maya’s result passes, because even under the most conservative defensible clustering (two-way) the interval still excludes zero. Had the two-way row crossed zero, the honest report would be “significant under state clustering but not under two-way clustering” — and then the result is fragile, and you say so.
Serial correlation over time. Maya’s panel runs over many years, and denial gaps are sticky — a county high this year tends to be high next year. That is exactly the within-unit serial correlation that the HAC / Newey–West estimator (Chapter 2.4) was built for, and that Bertrand, Duflo & Mullainathan (2004) showed will, if ignored, give a DiD a false-positive rate near 45% instead of 5%. We will treat their specific placebo construction in §2; for the SE flavor itself, the rule is that cluster-robust SEs that cluster by the unit already absorb arbitrary within-unit serial correlation (that is the whole point of the block-diagonal \boldsymbol\Omega), so a panel clustered by state is generally serially-correlation-robust without a separate HAC step. HAC is the tool when you have one long time series and cannot cluster.


The hard case: few clusters, and the wild cluster bootstrap
Now the threat that the table above silently hides, and the one Maya wrote into her threats table as “few-treated-cluster inference.” Cluster-robust standard errors lean on an asymptotic argument that needs the number of clusters to be large — the rule of thumb from Chapter 2.4 was 30 to 50. The danger is subtle: with few clusters, the cluster-robust SE is itself downward-biased and noisy, so the t-statistic does not follow the t-distribution you compare it against, and you over-reject — you find significance that is not there. Maya has 50 states, which sounds fine, but the relevant count for a treatment effect is closer to the number of treated clusters, and if only, say, eight states ever adopted an examination program, her effective cluster count is dangerously small. This is the same fragility that made Card & Krueger’s single-treated-state design (Chapter 4.1) demand permutation inference.
The fix is the wild cluster bootstrap (Cameron, Gelbach & Miller 2008),3 which you met by name in Chapter 2.4. The intuition is the trick worth revealing. An ordinary bootstrap resamples observations; that breaks the within-cluster correlation you are trying to respect. A cluster bootstrap resamples whole clusters; with few clusters that does not give you enough distinct resamples. The wild cluster bootstrap does something cleverer: it keeps the clusters and the regressors exactly as they are, and instead flips the sign of each cluster’s residuals at random — multiplying every residual in a cluster by +1 or -1 with equal probability (the Rademacher weights) — to manufacture a distribution of the test statistic under the null. You re-impose the null hypothesis (\beta = 0) when computing the residuals, perturb, re-estimate thousands of times, and read your real t-statistic’s position in that bootstrapped distribution to get a p-value. It is, in spirit, the same permutation logic as a placebo test: build the distribution of “what this statistic looks like when nothing is going on,” then locate your real number in it.
# Wild cluster bootstrap for the treatment coefficient, restricted (null-imposed) residuals.
# Pedagogical implementation; in practice use a vetted package (e.g., wildboottest / fwildclusterboot).
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

def wild_cluster_bootstrap(df, formula, param, cluster_col, B=1999, seed=8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # 1) Unrestricted fit -> the t-stat we actually observed.
    fit = smf.ols(formula, data=df).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df[cluster_col]}
    )
    t_obs = fit.params[param] / fit.bse[param]

    # 2) Restricted fit: impose H0 by dropping the tested regressor, keep its residuals.
    restricted_formula = formula.replace(f" + {param}", "").replace(f"{param} + ", "")
    r_fit = smf.ols(restricted_formula, data=df).fit()
    resid_hat = r_fit.resid.to_numpy()
    fitted_0  = r_fit.fittedvalues.to_numpy()
    yname = formula.split("~")[0].strip()

    clusters = df[cluster_col].to_numpy()
    uniq = np.unique(clusters)
    t_boot = np.empty(B)
    for b in range(B):
        # 3) One Rademacher (+/-1) draw PER CLUSTER, broadcast to its rows.
        signs = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=uniq.size)
        w = np.empty_like(resid_hat)
        for s, c in zip(signs, uniq):
            w[clusters == c] = s
        df_b = df.copy()
        df_b[yname] = fitted_0 + w * resid_hat        # bootstrap outcome under H0
        fb = smf.ols(formula, data=df_b).fit(
            cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df_b[cluster_col]}
        )
        t_boot[b] = fb.params[param] / fb.bse[param]

    # 4) Two-sided bootstrap p-value: how often |t_boot| >= |t_obs|.
    p = (np.sum(np.abs(t_boot) >= np.abs(t_obs)) + 1) / (B + 1)
    return t_obs, p


How to read pass/fail, and honesty
Pass: the wild-cluster p-value is small (and roughly agrees with your conventional clustered p-value). Your significance was not an artifact of too few clusters. Fail: the wild-cluster p-value is much larger — say your conventional table said p = 0.01 but the bootstrap says p = 0.18. That is the few-clusters illusion exposed, and the honest report is brutal and short: “The point estimate is −1.4pp, but with few treated clusters, inference is too imprecise to reject zero; we report the result as suggestive, not significant.” You do not get to keep the three stars from the conventional SE once the bootstrap has told you they are fake. The whole reason the wild cluster bootstrap is in your threats table is that, for designs with few treated clusters, it, not the default clustered SE, is the honest inference. If they disagree, believe the bootstrap.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
section: 2. Placebo tests: would this pattern appear where it can’t be real?
text:
2. Placebo tests: would this pattern appear where it can’t be real?
The second attack is the most intuitive and, when it fails, the most damning. A placebo test runs your exact analysis on a setting where, by construction, there can be no treatment effect — a fake treatment date, a fake treatment unit, a fake outcome — and checks that you correctly find nothing. The logic is the logic of a control group raised one level: if your method finds an “effect” where none can exist, then the “effect” it found in your real analysis is suspect too, because your method is manufacturing patterns out of whatever structure is in the data. Recall the placebo permutation inference of Chapter 4.1 (assign Card & Krueger’s treatment to every other state in turn) and the Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan placebo of Week 5: this is the same idea, now a standard weapon in your battery.

Fake treatment dates (the in-time placebo)
Maya picks a year well before any state actually adopted an examination program — say, three years before the earliest real adoption — and pretends the programs switched on then, leaving the true post-period out entirely so the fake effect cannot be contaminated by the real one. She re-runs the entire Callaway–Sant’Anna estimator on this fictional timing. What it probes: whether her estimator detects a “treatment effect” purely from the trend structure of the data — exactly the differential-pre-trend threat that sits in row one of her table. If adopting states were already on a different denial-gap trajectory, a fake treatment placed in the pre-period will catch that trajectory and report a spurious effect.
Pass: the placebo ATT is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. This is real, if asymmetric, support for parallel trends — it is the same evidence as a flat event-study lead, dressed as a single number. Fail: the placebo ATT is itself large and significant, perhaps even similar in size to the real estimate. That is close to fatal: it means your method finds “1.4pp effects” in years when nothing happened, so the 1.4pp it found in the real years carries no special weight. There is no spin that survives a failed in-time placebo; the honest move is to conclude the design cannot separate the treatment from a pre-existing trend, and either redesign (a cleaner control group, a shorter window) or report the result as uninterpretable.


Fake treatment units (the in-space placebo / permutation)
Now permute units instead of time. Assign fake “adoption” to states that never actually adopted, re-estimate, and repeat across many random reassignments to build a distribution of placebo effects. Locate the real effect in that distribution. What it probes: whether an effect of Maya’s magnitude shows up routinely when treatment is assigned at random — the synthetic-control-style inference of Chapter 4.4, and the right inference when clusters are too few for the t-approximation. Pass: the real effect sits in the extreme tail of the placebo distribution (say, more extreme than 95% of placebos), so a permutation p-value below 0.05. Fail: the real effect is buried in the middle of the placebo cloud — plenty of randomly-assigned “treatments” produce effects as big — so it is not distinguishable from noise. The placebo distribution is the honest summary of uncertainty here; if your real number is unremarkable within it, say so plainly.


Fake outcomes (the placebo outcome)
Pick an outcome the treatment should have no plausible channel to move, but that shares the same data structure — Maya might use the denial gap for a loan category exempt from fair-lending examination, or a gap that the program’s mechanism cannot touch. Pass: no effect on the placebo outcome, which rules out a broad confounder (a general economic shock to adopting states) that would have moved everything. Fail: the program “moves” an outcome it cannot mechanically affect — a tell that something other than the program is driving adopting states, and your effect is riding on it.
The unifying intellectual-honesty point: a placebo test is a prediction your theory makes about where you should find nothing, and reporting a failed placebo is not optional. Referees run placebos in their heads as they read; a paper that omits the obvious one reads as evasive, and a paper that reports a failed one and grapples with it reads as honest. You ran the placebo to find out the truth, not to collect a pass.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
section: 3. Sensitivity analysis: which knobs is my result hostage to?
text:
3. Sensitivity analysis: which knobs is my result hostage to?
Every analysis has knobs — tuning parameters and judgment calls that are individually defensible but, taken together, give you enormous freedom to land on a number you like. Sensitivity analysis wiggles each knob across its defensible range and reports how much the estimate moves. It overlaps with the specification curve of Chapter 8.1, but with a sharper question: not “is my result stable across all forks?” but “is my result hostage to this particular arbitrary choice?” Three knobs matter most.

Bandwidth (the RD knob)
This one is for the regression-discontinuity crowd (Chapter 4.3). An RD estimate is a comparison of units just above and just below a cutoff, and “just” is set by a bandwidth h: include units within h of the threshold. Too wide and you import units far from the cutoff whose comparison is contaminated by the very confounding RD was meant to avoid; too narrow and you have almost no data and a wild, imprecise estimate. The bias–variance trade-off is exactly the one the Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik robust bias-corrected procedure automates, but you must still show the estimate is not an artifact of one bandwidth. The standard display is a sensitivity plot: the RD coefficient and its confidence band as a function of h, from half the optimal bandwidth to twice it. Pass: the estimate is flat and stays significant across the range — the result is not a bandwidth artifact. Fail: the estimate swings wildly, or is significant only in a narrow window of h around the value you happened to pick. That is a result tuned into existence, and a referee who sees a single bandwidth with no sensitivity plot assumes the worst.


Controls (the specification knob)
How does the estimate move as you add or drop control variables? This is more subtle than “more controls is more rigorous,” and §4’s Oster logic will make the subtlety precise. For now the diagnostic is coefficient stability: report your estimate with no controls, with your primary controls, and with an aggressive battery of extra controls. Pass with a caveat: the coefficient barely moves as controls are added. That is suggestive of robustness — but read §4 before you celebrate, because stability alone can be a trap. Fail: the coefficient halves, or flips sign, when you add a control. Then the result depends entirely on a modeling choice, and you must justify which control set is correct on substantive grounds, not pick the one that keeps the stars. A special trap: never “control for” a variable that is itself an outcome of the treatment (a post-treatment variable / bad control), because that bleeds the effect away and the resulting instability is an artifact of the bad control, not evidence against your result.


Sample and winsorizing (the data knob)
Finally, the choices buried in data construction (Week 7’s Chapter 7.4). Does the result survive dropping the most extreme observations? Financial data is fat-tailed, and a single county or firm-year can move a coefficient; the conventional defense is winsorizing — capping each variable at, say, its 1st and 99th percentiles so extreme values are pulled to the cap rather than deleted. Sensitivity here means re-running at 0% (raw), 1%, and 5% winsorizing, and also dropping defensible subsamples (excluding the crisis years 2008–2009, excluding the largest state, excluding the earliest adoption cohort). Pass: the estimate is stable across these. Fail: the result lives or dies on a handful of outliers, or on including one influential state, or on the crisis window. Then the honest claim is narrower than the one you wanted: “the effect holds outside the financial crisis but is not separately identified within it,” for instance. Narrowing the claim to what the data actually support is not a defeat; it is the entire job.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
section: 4. Multiple-testing corrections, done right
text:
4. Multiple-testing corrections, done right
Maya does not have one outcome. Like most real projects she has a family: the denial gap overall, but also the gap in approval rates, in interest-rate spreads, in loan amounts, broken out by minority subgroup. Suppose she tests eight outcomes and two come back significant at the 5% level. How impressed should you be? Recall the hard lesson of Chapter 1.5: the false-positive rate of a single test does not protect a search across many tests. If all eight outcomes were truly null, the chance that at least one clears the 5% bar is 1 - (1-0.05)^8 \approx 0.34 — a one-in-three chance of a false “discovery” from pure noise. Run enough outcomes and a significant result is expected, not impressive. Maya owes the reader an adjustment for the size of her family.
The two corrections you must know — both named in Chapter 1.5 — answer two different questions, and using the wrong one is a common and consequential error.
Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate (FWER): the probability of even one false positive across the whole family. The rule is brutal and simple — test each of m hypotheses at \alpha/m instead of \alpha (equivalently, multiply each p-value by m and cap at 1). For Maya’s eight outcomes, the per-test bar becomes 0.05/8 = 0.00625. When to use it: when a single false positive is costly and you must be able to say “every starred result here is almost surely real” — a drug-approval mindset. The cost: Bonferroni is conservative to the point of bluntness; with a large family it kills statistical power, and you will fail to flag real effects (Type II errors) to buy near-certainty against any false one.
Benjamini–Hochberg (1995) controls the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected fraction of your declared discoveries that are false. This is usually the more sensible target when you are screening many candidate signals and can tolerate that, say, 5% of your “finds” are flukes — the natural posture in finance and in genomics, where BH was born. The procedure is a ranked one and worth seeing in full:

Order your m p-values from smallest to largest: p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}.
Find the largest rank k such that p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{m}\,\alpha.
Reject (declare significant) all hypotheses with rank \le k.

The genius is the sliding bar: the smallest p-value is held to the strict Bonferroni-like threshold \frac{1}{m}\alpha, but each successive p-value gets a more lenient bar, so a cluster of moderately-small p-values can reinforce each other into significance in a way Bonferroni would never allow. Find the largest k with p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{8}(0.05): that is k=2 (0.011 ≤ 0.0125). BH then declares the two smallest — denial gap and approval-rate gap — significant, and the rest not. Note the rate-spread gap at p=0.030, which cleared the naive 5% bar, does not survive: once you account for having looked at eight outcomes, it is no longer distinguishable from the noise you would expect from eight draws. Bonferroni here would have required p \le 0.00625 and kept only the primary denial gap; BH keeps two. That gap between them is the FWER-vs-FDR trade-off made concrete.
How to read pass/fail and stay honest. The non-negotiable rule: declare your family in advance — ideally in the pre-analysis plan of Chapter 7.3 — so you cannot gerrymander it after the fact. The cardinal sin is to run twenty outcomes, find one significant, and report it alone as if it were the only test you ran; that is the garden of forking paths from Chapter 1.5, and the correction exists precisely to disarm it. The honest report names m, names the correction, and states the surviving set: “Of the eight pre-specified outcomes, two survive Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control at 5%.” If your headline result is the one that fails to survive correction, you say so, and your contribution becomes “suggestive on the secondary outcomes, robust only on the primary.” A reader trusts a corrected family far more than an uncorrected lone star.

title: Ch 8.2 — Robustness & Inference Stress-Tests
section: 5. Oster (2019) δ: how much would the unobservable confounder have to matter?
text:
5. Oster (2019) δ: how much would the unobservable confounder have to matter?
Now the deepest attack, and the one with the most beautiful logic, because it confronts the threat that cannot be tested directly: an omitted variable you never measured. Maya’s weakest design assumption — the one in her threats table with the residual concern “unobserved creditworthiness differences could still shift the gap” — is selection on unobservables. No balance table can reach it, because the confounder you fear is by definition the one not in the table. So the question can never be “is there an unobserved confounder?” (there always could be). Oster (2019) reframes it into a question you can answer: how strong would selection on unobservables have to be, relative to the selection on observables you can see, to explain away your entire result? If the answer is “implausibly strong — stronger than the observables, which you already control for,” your result is robust to the threat you cannot test. If the answer is “barely as strong as the observables,” it is fragile.

The coefficient-stability-plus-R² logic
The argument builds on the coefficient-stability intuition from §3, but fixes its fatal flaw. The naive idea is: if my coefficient barely moves when I add controls, it must be robust to omitted variables too. Oster shows this is only half the story, and the missing half is the R^2. Adding a control can leave the coefficient stable for two opposite reasons: either the control truly does not matter (genuinely reassuring), or the control matters but is nearly uncorrelated with treatment (the coefficient is stable but the controls explain a lot of outcome variance — and an unobservable as predictive as those controls could still move the coefficient a lot). Coefficient movement is only meaningful relative to how much explanatory power the controls added. A coefficient that stays put while R^2 jumps from 0.10 to 0.55 is far more reassuring than one that stays put while R^2 barely rises — because in the first case the controls were powerful and the coefficient shrugged them off, while in the second the controls were toothless and proved nothing.
Oster formalizes this with three ingredients you read off two regressions:

The uncontrolled regression: coefficient \hat\beta_0 and R^2 value \tilde R_0 (Maya: treatment with no covariates).
The controlled regression: coefficient \hat\beta_1 and R^2 value \tilde R_1 (Maya: her full covariate-conditional spec).
A maximum R^2, R_{\max}: the R^2 a hypothetical regression on treatment plus all observables and all unobservables would attain. You cannot observe it, so you assume it — Oster’s evidence-based default is R_{\max} = 1.3\,\tilde R_1, capped at 1.0.

The key parameter is \delta (delta): the ratio of selection on unobservables to selection on observables. \delta = 1 means the unobservables are exactly as related to treatment as the observables you control for — the natural benchmark, because it says “the stuff I couldn’t measure is no more confounding than the stuff I could.” \delta = 2 means twice as confounding; \delta = 0.5 means half. There are two ways to use it, and you should report both.
Use 1 — the bounding set. Fix \delta at the benchmark \delta = 1 and solve for the bias-adjusted coefficient \beta^{\ast}: where your estimate would land if unobservable selection were exactly as strong as observable selection. This gives an identified set, conventionally the interval [\hat\beta_1, \beta^{\ast}]. Pass: the set excludes zero — even with confounding as strong as your observables, the effect stays the same sign and away from zero. Fail: the set contains zero — plausible unobserved confounding could fully explain your result.
Use 2 — the δ that kills it. Set \beta^{\ast} = 0 and solve for the \delta that would be required to drive your effect to zero. Call it \hat\delta. Pass: \hat\delta \ge 1 (Oster’s heuristic threshold), meaning an unobservable would have to be at least as confounding as everything you observed to explain away the result — usually an implausible thing to assert, since researchers typically control for the most obvious confounders, so the leftovers should be weaker, not stronger. The larger \hat\delta is, the more robust. Fail: \hat\delta < 1 — a confounder weaker than your observables could erase the effect, so the result is fragile.
# Oster (2019) delta: how much stronger must unobservable selection be than
# observable selection to drive the treatment coefficient to zero?
def oster_delta(beta0, R0, beta1, R1, Rmax=None, beta_target=0.0):
    """beta0,R0 = uncontrolled coef & R^2; beta1,R1 = controlled coef & R^2."""
    if Rmax is None:
        Rmax = min(1.3 * R1, 1.0)          # Oster's evidence-based default
    num = (beta1 - beta_target) * (R1 - R0)
    den = (beta0 - beta1) * (Rmax - R1)
    return num / den                        # delta to reach beta_target (default 0)

# Maya: coef moves only modestly (-2.2 -> -1.4) while R^2 climbs a lot (0.08 -> 0.42) => robust.
delta = oster_delta(beta0=-2.2, R0=0.08, beta1=-1.4, R1=0.42)
print(f"delta to explain away the effect: {delta:.2f}")   # ~ 4.72  (>> 1 : robust)


Reading Maya’s δ, and the honesty rule
Plug in Maya’s numbers: an uncontrolled ATT of −2.2 that moves only modestly to −1.4 when controls are added, while R^2 climbs a lot, from 0.08 to 0.42. The coefficient moved a little but the controls explained a great deal — and it is that contrast that matters — so \hat\delta \approx 4.7. An unobservable would have to be roughly four to five times as correlated with examination adoption as Maya’s full set of applicant-composition controls to explain away the effect. Since she already controls for the obvious confounders, an unobservable that potent is hard to argue for, and she can write: “The result is robust to selection on unobservables under the Oster (2019) test: an omitted confounder would have to be 4.7 times as important as the rich observables to nullify the estimate (\hat\delta = 4.7 \gg 1, with R_{\max} = 1.3\tilde R_1).”
Three honesty rules specific to Oster, because the test is easy to abuse:

Report R_{\max} and defend it. \hat\delta is mechanically sensitive to R_{\max}: assume the controls explain everything (R_{\max} = \tilde R_1) and the test is vacuous; assume R_{\max} = 1 and it is harshest. State which you used (default 1.3\tilde R_1) and show how \hat\delta moves if you push R_{\max} to 1. A δ reported without its R_{\max} is uninterpretable.
δ is not a p-value. It does not measure statistical significance; it measures robustness to a specific, untestable threat. A result can be wildly significant and have \hat\delta = 0.3 (fragile to confounding); another can have a modest t and \hat\delta = 5 (precise enough, hard to confound). Report both kinds of evidence — they answer different questions.
A failing δ is information, not an embarrassment. If \hat\delta = 0.4, the test has told you, honestly, that a confounder weaker than your observables could be the whole story. That belongs in your limitations, stated plainly: “We cannot rule out that unobserved selection drives the result; an omitted variable only 0.4 times as important as our controls would suffice.” This is the §5 honesty of the identification memo, made quantitative — you found the project’s vulnerability before a referee did, and you said so.

6. Assembling the battery, and what a survivor looks like
Step back and see the structure. Each test in this chapter answered a row of the threats table you wrote in Chapter 7.5:

A result that survives this battery is not proven — nothing observational ever is, as Chapter 7.5 hammered — but it is credible in the precise sense the identification memo demanded: you tried every attack a referee would try, you tried them on yourself first, and the number held. That is the strongest claim empirical work can honestly make.
And the converse is the real lesson of this chapter, so let it land. A result that does not survive should be reported as not surviving. The single most important professional habit you can build is to treat a failed robustness test as a finding, not a setback to be buried. If Maya’s wild cluster bootstrap had returned p = 0.2, the honest paper says the effect is suggestive but imprecisely estimated. If her in-time placebo had lit up, the honest paper says the design cannot separate the program from a pre-trend. If her Oster δ had come in at 0.4, the honest paper states that unobserved selection could explain the result. None of these is a failure of you; each is a success of the method, which is built to stop you from telling the world something that is not true. The author who runs these tests hoping they pass and the author who runs them hoping to learn the truth get the same code and the same output — but only the second one is doing science. The whole apparatus of this chapter exists to make you the second kind of author, on purpose, before anyone else gets the chance to make you one by force.

section: Your Turn
text:
Your Turn
Open nb8.2 — the robustness-battery harness. It is built to run column 3 of your threats table, end to end, on your pre-registered estimate from Chapter 8.1: a placebo engine (fake dates, fake units via permutation, fake outcomes), a standard-error panel that re-clusters at every defensible level and runs the wild cluster bootstrap, a Benjamini–Hochberg routine for your pre-specified family of outcomes, and an Oster δ calculator with an R_{\max} sensitivity sweep. Run each cell, read each pass/fail by the rules above, and assemble the results into the robustness table that becomes the backbone of your paper’s robustness section (the craft of presenting it lives in Chapter 8.3 and Appendix D.3).
Three reflection prompts to write up alongside the notebook:

Run your scariest placebo first. Take the threat you ranked most dangerous in your Chapter 7.5 table and build the placebo that would expose it — the fake date if you fear a pre-trend, the permutation if you fear few clusters, the fake outcome if you fear a broad confounder. Run it. If it fails, do not move on: write the honest sentence that narrows or kills your claim, and decide whether to redesign or to report the limitation plainly. A robustness section that only contains passes is not more credible — it is less, because a reader assumes you did not try hard enough to fail.
Read your coefficient stability with Oster’s eyes. Report your treatment coefficient with no controls and with your full controls, and also report the two R^2 values. Compute \hat\delta. Now answer the question §5 was built around: did your coefficient stay stable because the controls were powerful and it shrugged them off (large \hat\delta, reassuring), or because the controls were toothless (small \hat\delta, proves nothing)? Defend your R_{\max} choice, then re-run with R_{\max} = 1 and report how much \hat\delta moves.
Audit your family. Write down every outcome you have looked at — not just the ones you plan to report. How many is m? Apply both Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg. Which results survive each? If your headline result survives only the uncorrected single test and not the correction for your true family size, what is the honest contribution sentence you can write — and is it the one you were hoping to write?

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
text:
1. The shape of the paper
You have, by now, almost everything a paper is made of. You filed a pre-analysis plan (Ch 7.3) and distilled it into the one page the whole project defends — the identification memo of Ch 7.5. You executed the pre-registered specification and built the specification curve (Ch 8.1). You ran column 3 of your threats table for every row, turning each promised defense into an actual robustness result (Ch 8.2). What you have is a folder full of tables, a frozen point estimate, a defensible identifying assumption, and a pile of checks that survived. What you do not yet have is a paper. This chapter is about the last transformation: turning that folder into a piece of prose that a stranger — a busy, skeptical, slightly hostile stranger called a referee — reads in one sitting and comes away believing.
Here is the reveal, the thing this whole chapter turns on, stated before the details so you carry it through everything that follows. A paper is not a transcript of what you did; it is an argument for why a reader should believe what you found. Those are different objects. The transcript is chronological and exhaustive — first I downloaded HMDA, then I cleaned it, then I tried three specifications, two of which broke. The argument is logical and ruthlessly selective — here is the question, here is why my design answers it, here is the answer, here is why you cannot easily dismiss it. Beginning writers produce transcripts and wonder why nobody finishes them. The move from transcript to argument is the single most valuable skill this chapter teaches, and almost every rule below is a special case of it.
There is a second reveal layered under the first, and it is the reason Week 5 came before Week 8. You already know how to read a paper as a referee — tables first, identifying assumption second, prose last and skeptically. Writing the paper is just building the object you learned to attack, so that it survives your own Week-5 reading. Every section below maps onto a question your Reader’s-Guide anatomy taught you to ask. The introduction answers “what is the question and why should I care?” The design section answers “what is the identifying assumption, and would it hold?” The results section answers “what is the headline number?” You are not learning a new format. You are learning to write for the reader you already are.
Empirical-finance papers have a fixed skeleton, and the fixedness is a gift, not a constraint. A referee opening your manuscript knows exactly where to look for each thing, which means you do not get credit for being creative with the order — you only get penalized for hiding the introduction’s contribution in section 4. The standard order is: introduction, literature, data, empirical design / identification, results, robustness, conclusion, with tables and figures threaded through results and robustness and the bibliography at the back. Top journals vary the labels (some fold literature into the introduction, some call the design section “empirical strategy” or “research design”), but the load each section carries is invariant. Learn the loads, not the labels.
The proportions matter as much as the order. A common rookie error is a fifteen-page paper with a one-paragraph introduction and a six-page data section describing every variable in loving detail. Invert that instinct. The introduction is the most-read and most-rewritten part of the paper — many referees decide whether to recommend acceptance from the introduction alone, then read the rest looking for reasons to confirm that snap judgment. The data section, by contrast, should be efficient: enough that the work is reproducible, not so much that it buries the argument. Spend your writing time where the reader spends their attention, and the reader spends it at the front.
One structural principle unifies the whole document: say the important thing first, at every scale. The paper leads with its contribution. The introduction leads with the hook. The results section leads with the headline table. Each paragraph leads with its topic sentence. A reader who quits after the first sentence of any unit should still have learned the most important thing in that unit. This is the opposite of how you were taught to write a mystery-novel essay in high school, building suspense toward a reveal at the end. In a paper, suspense is a bug. The reader is not your entertainment; they are your judge, and you make their job easy by front-loading every verdict.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 2. The introduction that promises
text:
2. The introduction that promises
The introduction is a promise machine. In roughly four to six paragraphs it must make a specific reader want to read the rest, and it does that by promising — credibly — that the payoff is worth their next twenty minutes. There is a near-canonical structure that the best empirical papers follow almost mechanically, and you should follow it too until you have earned the right to deviate. It has four moves: the hook, the one-sentence contribution, the “we find” preview, and the roadmap. Take them in order.
The hook. The first paragraph names the question and makes the reader care, in that order, fast. It opens with a real-world fact or tension — a number, a puzzle, a policy debate — not with “the literature has long studied.” Maya’s hook is not “fair lending has been studied since the 1970s.” It is closer to: In 2023, mortgage applicants from minority neighborhoods were denied at nearly twice the rate of applicants from white neighborhoods — a gap that persists even among applicants with similar incomes and loan sizes. Whether that gap reflects differential treatment, and whether policy can move it, is both a live regulatory question and an unresolved empirical one. Two sentences and the reader knows the stakes are real, the question is contested, and an answer would matter. The hook earns the reader’s attention with consequence, not with a literature recitation.
The one-sentence contribution. This is the sentence everything else serves, and it deserves its own subsection below — for now, know that it lands in the first or second paragraph and says, in one sentence, what this paper adds that did not exist before you wrote it. Not what you did (“we run a difference-in-differences on HMDA”) but what is now known that was not (“we provide the first causally credible estimate of how state fair-lending examination programs affect the minority–white mortgage-denial gap”). The difference between those two formulations is the difference between a paper that gets read and one that gets desk-rejected.
The “we find” preview. Having promised a contribution, you must immediately pay a deposit on it: tell the reader the answer. A paragraph, usually beginning literally “We find that…” or “Our main result is…,” that previews the headline number, its sign, its rough magnitude, and the key robustness fact. We find that adopting a fair-lending examination program reduces the county-level minority–white denial gap by about 1.8 percentage points, roughly a fifth of the pre-period gap; the effect emerges within two years of adoption, is robust to alternative control groups and clustering, and survives a placebo test that randomly reassigns adoption years. Students resist this. They feel they are “spoiling the ending.” Reread §1: there is no ending to spoil. A referee who has to hunt through nine pages to find out what you found is a referee who is already annoyed with you. Give the number up front; you will spend the rest of the paper earning the right to have stated it.
The roadmap. The introduction’s last paragraph is a short, functional map: “Section 2 positions our work in the literature; Section 3 describes the HMDA data; Section 4 lays out the difference-in-differences design and our identifying assumption; Section 5 presents the main results; Section 6 reports robustness; Section 7 concludes.” A few sentences, no drama. Some venues consider the explicit roadmap old-fashioned, but for a student paper it is a safe, professional default — it signals that you know the genre.
A discipline that spans all four moves: the introduction should be readable by someone who will never read the rest of the paper. A program officer skimming fifty abstracts, a professor deciding whether to assign your paper, a journalist looking for a number to quote — all of them stop at the introduction. Write it so that a reader who stops there walks away with the question, the answer, and the appropriate degree of confidence. If your introduction only makes sense after one has read your results, it has failed at its one job.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 3. The one-sentence contribution
text:
3. The one-sentence contribution
Stop and build this sentence on its own, because if you cannot write it, you do not yet have a paper — you have a regression and a hope, the same diagnosis the identification memo gave you about the identifying assumption. The one-sentence contribution is the answer to a question a skeptical reader is entitled to ask and will ask: what is true now, that was not established before you did this work? It is the reason the paper exists. Everything else — the data, the design, the forty robustness checks — is in service of making this one sentence believable, exactly as the whole paper is in service of the identifying-assumption sentence. The two sentences are cousins: one states what you claim to have found, the other states the condition under which the claim is true.
A good contribution sentence usually does one of a small number of recognizable jobs, and naming the job helps you write the sentence. You might be the first to credibly estimate a specific effect (“we provide the first quasi-experimental estimate of…”). You might overturn or qualify an established finding (“we show that the widely cited X effect disappears once Y is accounted for”). You might reconcile two conflicting literatures, measure a mechanism the literature had only speculated about, or bring new data to an old question (“using transaction-level on-chain data, we…”). Pick the job honestly. The fastest way to a referee’s contempt is a contribution sentence that claims the “first” job when three prior papers did the same thing, which is exactly what your literature review is about to either support or expose.
Calibrate the verb to the evidence — this is the causal-language discipline of §7, previewed here because it bites first in this sentence. If your design is a clean staggered DiD with flat pre-trends, you have earned “credibly estimate.” If your design is OLS on observables with a plausible omitted variable you could not rule out, you have not, and your contribution sentence says “document a robust association,” “provide suggestive evidence,” or “establish a new stylized fact” — never “show that X causes Y.” The reading guides of Week 5 trained you to catch authors who overclaim in exactly this sentence. The grader of your paper is running the same check. Match the verb to the design, and run the check on yourself before anyone else does.
A practical test: hand your one-sentence contribution to a classmate who has not seen your project and ask them to tell you, from that sentence alone, what you did and why it matters. If they can, the sentence works. If they ask “wait, what’s the question?” or “is that causal?”, the sentence is doing the introduction’s whole job badly, and no amount of polish on paragraphs four through forty will fix it.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 4. The literature review that positions
text:
4. The literature review that positions
Here is where most student papers go wrong, and the failure has a name: the annotated bibliography. That is the literature review that reads “Smith (2018) finds A. Jones (2020) finds B. Garcia (2021) finds C. We contribute to this literature.” It is a list. It does the reader no work. It tells them what exists but not where the hole is, and the hole is the only thing the section exists to reveal. A list of prior work is to a literature review what a transcript is to a paper — the raw material, mistaken for the finished argument.
A literature review does exactly one job: it draws a map of what is known so that the gap you fill is visible as a gap. The reader should finish the section able to point at empty space on the map and say “ah — that is what nobody has done, and that is what this paper does.” You build that map by grouping and contrasting, not by enumerating. Cluster the prior work into two or three strands — by question, by method, or by finding — and characterize each strand by what it established and what it could not. “One strand documents the raw denial gap (Bartlett et al.; the HMDA descriptive literature) but cannot separate differential treatment from differential applicant composition. A second strand uses audit studies to isolate treatment but cannot speak to the population-scale effect of policy. We sit at the intersection: population-scale HMDA data and a policy shock that lets us identify a treatment effect.” Now the gap is not asserted; it is constructed, brick by brick, out of the literature itself.
Three rules keep the section honest and sharp. First, every paper you cite should be load-bearing — it either builds part of the map’s wall or marks the edge of the hole. If a citation could be deleted without changing where the gap appears, delete it; a padded literature review signals that you are counting references rather than building an argument. Second, be generous to the work you build on and precise about its limits, never dismissive. “Prior work was wrong” is the voice of someone who has not read carefully and is about to be refereed by the author they just insulted. “Prior work established X under conditions Y; we extend to the case where Y fails” is the voice of someone who belongs in the conversation. Third, position, do not summarize. The reader does not need a book report on each paper; they need to know its coordinate on your map. One sentence per paper, often less, with the contrast doing the work.
This section is also where Weeks 5 and 6 cash out. You read Fama–French, Jegadeesh–Titman, Petersen, Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan, the fair-lending and innovation literatures, precisely so you would know which conversations exist and where the live arguments are. A literature review is you reporting back from those conversations and announcing where you intend to speak. Cite primary sources with full bibliographic information per CONVENTIONS §6, and if you cannot verify a citation, tag it [CHECK] rather than fabricate it — a hallucinated reference is the one error a referee can catch in ten seconds and never forgive.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 5. Data, design, and results
text:
5. Data, design, and results
These three sections are the body of the paper — the place where the promise of the introduction is redeemed with actual evidence. Each has a specific load to carry, and a specific failure mode to avoid.
The data section makes the work reproducible without burying the argument. It names the source and vintage (HMDA LAR, a pinned snapshot date per CONVENTIONS §5), the sample (which years, which units, which filters and why each filter was applied — every exclusion is a potential selection threat, so disclose it), the unit of observation, and the construction of the key variables. It carries one near-mandatory artifact: a summary-statistics table (means, standard deviations, counts, by treatment status where relevant) that lets a reader sanity-check the sample before trusting anything built on it. What the data section does not do is narrate your cleaning ordeal. The reader does not need to know that the 2018 file had a malformed column; they need to know the final sample and how to rebuild it. Put the ordeal in the replication packet (Ch 8.5) and the appendix, not the paper.
The empirical design / identification section puts the identifying assumption front and center. This section is, in large part, your Ch 7.5 identification memo turned into prose, and that is by design — the identifying-assumption paragraph you wrote there becomes this section nearly verbatim. State the specification in the CONVENTIONS §4 form: outcome, treatment, controls, fixed effects, clustering, sample, and the identifying assumption in one sentence. Write the estimating equation explicitly. For Maya, the staggered group-time formulation she committed to:

\text{Gap}_{ct} = \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \,\mathbb{1}[t - G_s = k] + \boldsymbol{\delta}'\mathbf{X}_{ct} + \alpha_c + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{ct},

where \text{Gap}_{ct} is the county-year minority–white denial gap, G_s is the year state s adopted its examination program, \alpha_c and \lambda_t are county and year fixed effects, and standard errors are clustered by state. Then — and this is the heart of the section — state the assumption that makes \beta_k for k \geq 0 a causal effect rather than a correlation: absent the programs, adopting and never-adopting states’ denial gaps would have moved in parallel. Name the threat, name the design feature that addresses it, in the same breath. This is CONVENTIONS §4 and the entire ethic of the identification memo, now load-bearing in the paper. A design section that says “we control for confounders” instead of naming the assumption has thrown away the one thing that makes the paper credible.
The results section leads with the headline table. Open with the single table that contains your main estimate — for Maya, the overall ATT and the event-time profile from the clean Callaway–Sant’Anna estimator. Walk the reader through it in prose: point at the coefficient, state its sign, its magnitude in units a human can feel (1.8 percentage points, “a fifth of the pre-period gap” — not just a number), and its statistical precision. The cardinal sin here is the “data dump”: a results section that presents eight tables with equal weight and lets the reader find the important one. You found it for them in the introduction; do it again here. Lead with the headline, interpret it economically (is the effect big enough to matter, not just big enough to be significant?), and only then present the supporting and secondary results. Significance is not the same as importance — a coefficient can be three-starred and economically trivial — and your prose must carry the economic interpretation that the stars cannot.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 6. Robustness and conclusion
text:
6. Robustness and conclusion
The robustness section converts your threats table into persuasion. You already did the work in Chapter 8.2 — the placebos, the alternative standard errors, the bandwidth and control and sample perturbations, the Oster (2019) \delta for selection on unobservables. The writing task is to present those checks as answers to the specific threats your design section raised, not as a context-free pile of extra regressions. The organizing move is to mirror the threats-and-responses table from your identification memo: each subsection of robustness takes one named threat and shows the check that addresses it, with the residual concern stated plainly. “A reader might worry that the result is driven by anticipation; we re-estimate excluding the year before adoption and the effect is unchanged (Table 5).” That sentence does three things — names the threat, reports the check, states the reassuring result — and it does them in the reader’s order, the order in which they would attack the paper. Robustness sections that persuade are organized around the reader’s doubts, not around the author’s available regressions. Appendix D.3 gives the detailed standard for this; the principle is that a robustness check no one asked for persuades no one, while a check that answers a threat a referee was about to raise disarms the attack before it lands.
The conclusion says what we learned, what we cannot claim, and what comes next. It is not a summary that repeats the introduction — the reader just read the paper; they do not need a recap. It is a recalibration. First, a tight restatement of the finding in its properly hedged form. Second — and this is the part students skip, to their cost — an honest statement of limitations: the residual concerns from your threats table, the populations your sample does not cover, the mechanism you measured an effect on but could not fully open up. The conclusion is where the residual-concern column of your identification memo finally appears in the paper’s prose, and stating it is not weakness; it is the candor that makes a referee trust everything else. Third, “what’s next”: the question your paper opened but did not close, the natural extension, the data that would settle the residual concern. A conclusion that admits limits and points forward reads as the work of someone who sees their project clearly. A conclusion that claims the question is now permanently settled reads as the work of someone who has not yet been refereed.
There is a temptation, in the conclusion, to let the verbs creep back up — to write “this paper proves” or “we have established that” after eleven pages of disciplined hedging. Resist it. The conclusion is the most-quoted part of the paper after the abstract, and a single overclaiming sentence there can undo the calibrated honesty of everything before it.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 7. Causal-language discipline
text:
7. Causal-language discipline
Run a thread back through every section above: the contribution sentence, the design section, the results, the conclusion all live or die on whether you matched your verbs to your evidence. This deserves its own treatment because it is the discipline most often broken and most ruthlessly punished, and because you have been trained to enforce it on others since Week 5.
The rule is simple to state. Your strongest verb is bounded by your weakest assumption. A clean randomized experiment earns “causes,” “increases,” “the effect of.” A quasi-experiment with a testable-and-passed identifying assumption (a DiD with flat pre-trends, an RD with a smooth density) earns “causally estimate,” “the program reduced,” with the assumption named. An observational regression on observables — OLS with a plausible omitted variable you could not rule out — earns only “is associated with,” “predicts,” “is consistent with,” “suggestive of.” A descriptive or predictive study (Sam’s momentum sort, Fama–French) earns “documents,” “captures variation in,” and must not be dressed in causal clothing at all. The verb is a promise about the design, and a reader who knows designs reads your verbs as a confession of how strong yours is.
The most common failure is not lying; it is drift. The abstract hedges correctly (“we document a robust association”), the introduction is a little bolder (“our results suggest that the program reduces the gap”), the results section forgets itself (“the program reduces the gap by 1.8 points”), and the conclusion goes all the way (“we have shown that fair-lending examinations cause a decline in discrimination”). Each step is small; the cumulative drift is a paper that claims far more than its design supports. Guard against drift with a deliberate pass: after a draft is done, read only the verbs attached to your main result, in every section, and force them all down to the level your weakest assumption permits. This is exactly the audit your Week-5 reading guides ran on published authors — the one where you underlined every causal verb and asked “did the design earn this?” Run it on yourself.
Hedge appropriately, but do not over-hedge into mush — that is the opposite failure. A paper drowning in “may possibly perhaps under certain conditions tentatively suggest” has hedged itself out of any claim at all, and a referee cannot tell what you are actually asserting. Calibration cuts both ways: claim exactly as much as your design supports, no more and no less. If you ran a clean DiD with flat pre-trends and a battery of passed robustness checks, you have earned a confident “the program reduced the gap, and this estimate is credible under parallel trends” — say it, plainly, with the assumption attached. The discipline is not timidity; it is precision.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 8. Table and figure craft (and where the real standard lives)
text:
8. Table and figure craft (and where the real standard lives)
Referees read tables before they read prose. You learned this as a consumer in Week 5 — go to the tables first, find the headline number, read the prose last and skeptically. As a producer, the implication is stark: your tables must stand alone, because they are read first and sometimes read only. A reader should be able to understand your main table — what the sample is, what the coefficient means, what the stars and the parenthetical numbers indicate, what fixed effects and clustering were used — without leaving the table to hunt through your prose. A table that requires the surrounding paragraphs to be intelligible is a table that fails its first and most important reader.
That self-containment comes from a small number of craft elements, and here I will state the principles and then point you, deliberately, to where the detailed standard lives. The principles: a table has an informative title and complete notes that define the sample, the units, the estimator, and every symbol; coefficients report standard errors or t-statistics in parentheses directly beneath them, with the flavor of standard error named (classical, HC1/HC2/HC3, HAC, clustered — and clustered on what); significance stars are defined in the notes, never left to the reader’s guess; numbers carry a consistent and sensible number of significant digits (a coefficient is not more precise for having six decimal places); and the fixed effects, controls, sample size, and within-R^2 are disclosed in dedicated rows so the reader can see the specification at a glance. Figures follow the same ethic: an event-study plot shows point estimates and confidence intervals, labels its axes in real units, marks the reference period, and is legible in grayscale.
The full standard — exact table layout, what belongs in notes versus the main text, how to report R^2 versus within-R^2, how many digits for which kind of number, the precise FE-and-cluster disclosure lines, the prose-style rules for hedging and citation — lives in Appendix D (book/appendices/D-style-guide/), and you should treat it as the binding spec for your manuscript. D.1 covers table layout and notes; D.2 covers which coefficients to report and the FE/cluster/sample disclosure; D.3 covers robustness sections and the threats-and-responses table; D.4 covers the replication packet; D.5 covers prose style and causal-language discipline. This chapter tells you why tables must stand alone and lead the results; Appendix D tells you exactly how to build one that does. Do not reinvent the standard here — point your manuscript at D and follow it. And do not hand-format your tables in a text editor: the notebook does it for you, which is where this chapter is headed.

title: Chapter 8.3 — Writing the Empirical Paper (and the Abstract Your Poster Carries)
section: 9. A worked intro skeleton: Maya’s fair-lending DiD
text:
9. A worked intro skeleton: Maya’s fair-lending DiD
Let us assemble the four moves of §2 into an actual introduction skeleton, for the project Maya has carried since Week 1 and whose identification memo you read in Ch 7.5: a staggered difference-in-differences asking whether state fair-lending examination programs reduced the county-level minority–white mortgage-denial gap, pointed at the HMDA data Prof. Gao and his coauthor used to study how same-sex couples were treated when they applied to borrow.1 Read it as a fill-in-the-blanks template you can adapt to your own project; the bracketed labels name the move each paragraph is making.

[HOOK] In 2023, mortgage applicants in majority-minority neighborhoods were denied at nearly twice the rate of applicants in majority-white neighborhoods, a gap that narrows but does not vanish once income and loan size are held fixed. Whether such gaps reflect differential treatment by lenders — and whether supervisory policy can move them — is simultaneously a live question for fair-lending regulators and an unresolved empirical one, because the raw gap confounds how applicants are treated with who applies.
[CONTRIBUTION] This paper provides the first quasi-experimental estimate of how state fair-lending examination programs affect the county-level minority–white mortgage-denial gap, exploiting the staggered timing with which states adopted these programs as a source of plausibly exogenous variation in supervisory intensity.
[“WE FIND” PREVIEW] We find that adopting an examination program reduces the county-level denial gap by approximately 1.8 percentage points — about one-fifth of the pre-adoption gap — with effects emerging within two years of adoption and stabilizing thereafter. The estimate is robust to using only never- and not-yet-treated states as controls, to alternative clustering, and to a placebo test that randomly reassigns adoption years; pre-treatment event-study leads are flat and statistically indistinguishable from zero, consistent with the parallel-trends assumption on which our interpretation rests.
[POSITIONING, one bridge sentence into the literature] Our work sits at the intersection of two literatures that have not met: a descriptive HMDA literature that measures the denial gap but cannot separate treatment from composition, and an audit-study literature that isolates differential treatment but cannot speak to the population-scale effect of policy.
[ROADMAP] Section 2 positions our contribution in these literatures; Section 3 describes the HMDA sample and the construction of the denial gap; Section 4 presents the staggered difference-in-differences design and states our identifying assumption; Section 5 reports the main results; Section 6 presents robustness checks organized around the threats to identification; Section 7 concludes.

Read that skeleton against §3 and §7. The contribution sentence claims the “first quasi-experimental estimate” job and uses the verb “exploiting… plausibly exogenous variation” — a calibrated claim, not “we prove discrimination.” The preview gives the number, the magnitude in human units, the timing, and the key robustness fact, then immediately names the assumption it rests on (“consistent with the parallel-trends assumption”). The positioning sentence constructs the gap by contrast, not by listing. The hook leads with a fact and a tension, not with “the literature.” Every verb is bounded by the weakest assumption — parallel trends, untestable beyond the pre-period — so nowhere does the prose say “causes” without the conditional attached. That is the discipline of this entire chapter, compressed into five paragraphs. Your introduction will be longer and fuller, but if it makes these five moves, in this order, with verbs this honest, it will do its one job: promise a reader something worth their twenty minutes, and promise only what your design can deliver.

Your Turn
Open nb8.3 — “Publication-quality tables and figures.” This notebook takes the regression objects you produced in Chapters 8.1 and 8.2 — your pyfixest/linearmodels results, your event-study coefficients — and renders them into the publication-quality tables and figures your paper needs: a stargazer-style regression table and an event-study plot, both exported to LaTeX, both built to the Appendix D standard (named standard errors, defined stars, disclosed fixed effects and clustering, sensible significant digits, legible-in-grayscale figures). You will not hand-format a single table; the notebook does it, reproducibly, from the frozen results — which is the whole point. The tables you put in the paper are generated from the analysis, never retyped, so they can never silently drift from the numbers they claim to report.
Three reflection prompts to write up alongside the notebook:

Write your one-sentence contribution, then stress-test it. Hand it to a classmate who has not seen your project and ask them to tell you, from that sentence alone, what you did and why it matters. If they cannot, the sentence is failing the introduction’s central job. Which of the recognizable “jobs” from §3 does your contribution claim — first, overturn, reconcile, mechanism, new data — and does your literature review actually support that claim, or expose it?
Audit your verbs against your weakest assumption. Draft your “we find” preview paragraph. Now read only the verbs attached to your main result and force every one down to the level your weakest identifying assumption permits (§7). Did you write “causes” where “is associated with” was warranted? Did you over-hedge into mush where a confident, assumption-conditioned claim was earned? Rewrite until the verbs match the design exactly.
Make your headline table stand alone. Take the main table nb8.3 generates and cover up the surrounding prose. Can a reader who sees only the table determine the sample, the estimator, the meaning of the coefficient, what the stars mean, and what fixed effects and clustering were used? List every thing they cannot determine — then fix it in the table notes, following Appendix D, not in the paragraph.
