section: 7. Compile to PDF — only if a LaTeX engine exists
text:
7. Compile to PDF — only if a LaTeX engine exists
Here is the gate. Compiling requires a TeX engine, and we will not assume one is installed. We probe for tectonic, latexmk, and pdflatex with shutil.which(...) — the standard, cross-platform way to ask “is this command on the PATH?” — and:

If an engine is found, we run it as a subprocess against main.tex in the build dir, check the return code and that a main.pdf appeared, and report success.
If no engine is found, we do not fail. We print a clear message explaining that the compile is skipped, that the .tex is fully assembled and ready, and that it can be built on Overleaf or the camp container. The notebook exits cleanly either way.

This is the difference between a notebook that works on the instructor’s fully-provisioned machine and one that works on thirty student laptops. The durable artifact is the .tex plus its generated table and figure; the PDF is the icing that some machines can produce and some cannot.

# --- Gate the PDF compile on the presence of a LaTeX engine ------------------
def find_latex_engine():
    """Return (name, path) of the first available engine, or (None, None)."""
    for engine in ("tectonic", "latexmk", "pdflatex"):
        path = shutil.which(engine)
        if path:
            return engine, path
    return None, None

def compile_pdf(engine, tex_path):
    """Run the chosen engine on tex_path inside its directory. Returns CompletedProcess."""
    workdir = tex_path.parent
    name = tex_path.name
    if engine == "tectonic":
        cmd = ["tectonic", name]
    elif engine == "latexmk":
        cmd = ["latexmk", "-pdf", "-interaction=nonstopmode", name]
    else:  # pdflatex -- run twice so \ref/\label resolve
        cmd = ["pdflatex", "-interaction=nonstopmode", name]
    return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=workdir, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=180)

engine, engine_path = find_latex_engine()
pdf_path = BUILD_DIR / "main.pdf"

if engine is None:
    print("No LaTeX engine found on PATH (looked for tectonic, latexmk, pdflatex).")
    print("Skipping the PDF compile -- this is NOT an error.")
    print("The manuscript is fully assembled at:")
    print("   ", PAPER_TEX)
    print("It is ready to build on Overleaf or the camp container, e.g.:")
    print("    latexmk -pdf main.tex      # or:  tectonic main.tex")
    pdf_built = False
else:
    print(f"Found LaTeX engine: {engine}  ({engine_path})")
    try:
        proc = compile_pdf(engine, PAPER_TEX)
        if engine == "pdflatex" and pdf_path.exists():
            proc = compile_pdf(engine, PAPER_TEX)   # second pass for cross-refs
        pdf_built = pdf_path.exists() and proc.returncode == 0
        if pdf_built:
            print(f"Compiled successfully -> {pdf_path}  ({pdf_path.stat().st_size} bytes)")
        else:
            # A failed compile on a provisioned machine is worth surfacing, but the
            # assembled .tex remains the deliverable, so we do not raise.
            print(f"Compile returned code {proc.returncode}; PDF not produced.")
            print("Last 25 lines of engine output:")
            print("\n".join(proc.stdout.splitlines()[-25:]))
    except (subprocess.TimeoutExpired, OSError) as exc:
        print(f"Compile attempt failed ({exc!r}); the assembled .tex remains the deliverable.")
        pdf_built = False

print("\nLATEX_ENGINE_FOUND =", engine is not None)
print("PDF_BUILT          =", pdf_built)

section: 8. The Markdown → PDF path (pandoc), gated the same way
text:
8. The Markdown → PDF path (pandoc), gated the same way
LaTeX is not the only road to a PDF. Many writers draft in Markdown and let pandoc convert Markdown → LaTeX → PDF in one step. We mention it here, and gate it identically, because the same “generate, don’t paste” discipline applies: a pandoc build would ![](figures/event_study.png) the generated figure and pull the results in from a generated Markdown or LaTeX table, never from a typed number.
We probe for pandoc with shutil.which(...). If it is present we note the exact one-liner that would build the paper; if not, we print the skip message. Either way the notebook does not fail — the point is to show the gated pattern, so a student on any machine knows the command and knows it is safe to run when the tool exists.

# --- Markdown -> PDF via pandoc, gated on availability (mirror of the LaTeX gate) ---
pandoc_path = shutil.which("pandoc")

if pandoc_path is None:
    print("pandoc not found on PATH -- skipping the Markdown->PDF path (NOT an error).")
    print("When pandoc (and a PDF engine) are installed, the one-liner is:")
    print("    pandoc paper.md -o paper.pdf --pdf-engine=tectonic")
    print("It would embed the SAME generated figure/table, never a pasted number.")
    PANDOC_FOUND = False
else:
    print(f"Found pandoc ({pandoc_path}); the Markdown->PDF one-liner would be:")

title: Capstone Gallery — Exemplar Papers Behind the ASSIP Poster Deliverable
text:
Read this first: every result here is synthetic
This gallery holds five complete, publication-style exemplar papers — full ~3,400–4,800-word research narratives that show what “done” looks like at full size, before the distillation onto a 48”×36” poster and into a 200–300-word JSSR abstract that ASSIP actually grades.
Each paper runs from abstract to honest limits the way a real empirical-finance paper does: a question worth asking, a literature it sits inside, a dataset, a stated identifying assumption, a headline table, robustness organized around the threats, and a conclusion that says plainly what the design cannot establish. They exist so that before you build your own poster, you can study what the full narrative behind a poster looks like, instead of inferring it from a rubric.
Each paper is paired with an annotated commentary — a “How this paper was built” section at the end — that narrates every choice against the camp’s conventions and the Appendix-D table-and-prose standard: why the standard errors are clustered this way and not that, why the identifying assumption is phrased as one sentence, why a verb was softened from “causes” to “is associated with.” The paper shows you the finished object; the commentary shows you the decisions that produced it. Read both — and then, before you sit down to draft your own poster, do the exercise in your head: which sentence of this paper is the question panel? which is the design panel? which sentence of the abstract is “we find”? That is the translation Lab 8 makes you perform on your own work.
All quantitative results in these five papers are synthetic and illustrative. They were constructed for instruction — built to be consistent with the relevant Week-6 notebooks and seeded so they regenerate bit-for-bit — and they are NOT empirical findings. No coefficient, standard error, sample size, correlation, or figure in this gallery describes a real lender, a real firm, a real patent, a real filing, or a real market. Several of the datasets are built with a known, planted truth precisely so the method can be checked against a ground truth that no real dataset gives you — that is the whole point of a synthetic study (Lab 4’s slogan: when you are unsure whether a method does what it claims, build a universe where you know the truth and check).
Read these papers for their craft — the structure, the table design, the calibrated verbs, the disciplined hedging, the honest limits — and copy the craft, never the numbers. Where a real paper would name a data vintage, a journal, or a statute, an exemplar says so and stops. Where a citation could not be verified, it is tagged [CHECK] rather than fabricated, exactly as the conventions require. Every paper carries its own synthetic-data notice at the top; this one governs the whole gallery.

section: The five capstones
text:
The five capstones
Each paper is tied to a dataset track and to a Gao or anchor paper that defines its question, so you can trace the line from a published study to a camp-scale reproduction.

Fair Lending on HMDA — Track: mortgage-denial decomposition · Anchor: Sun & Gao (2019) · Notebook: nb6.4. How much of the minority/non-minority mortgage-denial gap survives the legitimate underwriting controls? A Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition on a synthetic, HMDA-like panel with a planted amount of discrimination, used to show exactly how an omitted credit score inflates the residual and how over-controlling on a pricing channel collapses it. The model paper for the selection-on-observables discipline: a residual is a bounded, fragile number, not a verdict.
Common Ownership from 13F — Track: institutional-holdings overlap · Anchor: Gao, Han, Kim & Pan (2024), “Overlapping institutional ownership along the supply chain and earnings management of supplier firms,” Journal of Corporate Finance, 84, 102520. When the same institutions hold large stakes in competing firms, does it change how much those firms voluntarily disclose? Builds a firm-pair common-ownership measure from synthetic 13F-like holdings and runs a panel fixed-effects regression of a disclosure index on peer common ownership. The exemplar for disciplined observational work: the association survives the most demanding specification, and the paper refuses to call it causal. Note: this is a student-track variant — the anchor paper’s actual outcome is supplier-firm earnings management (discretionary accruals); the capstone substitutes voluntary disclosure as a sibling outcome that is easier to build at camp scale. See the variant notice at the top of the capstone.
Innovation from USPTO PatentsView — Track: market-based innovation measurement · Anchor: Kogan, Papanikolaou, Seru & Stoffman (2017) · Notebook: nb6.1. What is a single patent worth? Reconstructs the KPSS measure — the abnormal stock return in a three-day window around a patent’s grant, scaled by market cap — on a seeded synthetic panel where the true patent value is known. Recovers the planted value, validates it against next-year profitability, and shows how contaminating news in the grant window degrades the measure. The model for turning an unobservable into an observable and checking the recovery.
SEC 8-K Text Classification — Track: AI / text-as-data module · Notebook: nb6.5 · Out-of-sample validated. Can a classifier recover the type of event an 8-K reports from its text, and does the short-window return reaction differ by type? Treats the classifier as a measurement instrument, not an oracle: hand-labels a gold set, freezes the rubric against a held-out test split before any returns are examined, and reports out-of-sample precision/recall/F1 and Cohen’s κ. The exemplar for using an LLM in research honestly — with the training-data-leakage audit and full prompt disclosure that applied work too often skips.
FRED Macro Event Study — Track: macro-announcement event study · Anchor: Kuttner (2001); Bernanke & Kuttner (2005). Do FOMC surprises move the market? Separates the expected component of each rate decision from its surprise and regresses the announcement-day equity return on the surprise, with HAC (Newey–West) standard errors, placebo dates, and split-sample checks. The model for the full event-study scaffolding from free data — and for reporting an “announcement-day association” under a tightly defended timing assumption rather than overclaiming a causal effect.

section: How to use the gallery
text:
How to use the gallery
These papers are working documents, not display pieces. Three ways to put them to work:
Read them like a referee. Bring the Week-5 anatomy of a journal paper to bear: take each one apart section by section — does the introduction state a contribution, is the identifying assumption a single defensible sentence, does the robustness section answer the threats it names, does the conclusion concede what the design cannot reach? Practice the skeptical read before you ask anyone to give your own poster that read. (See Week 5: Anatomy of a Journal Paper.)
Model your own poster’s structure on them. When you build your ASSIP poster, use the matching exemplar as a structural source for the distillation: the question panel comes from the paper’s hook + one-sentence contribution; the design panel comes from the paper’s identification section (the identifying-assumption sentence in contract form); the headline panel pulls a figure straight from the paper’s results; the robustness panel pulls the specification curve; the contribution-and-limits panel compresses the paper’s conclusion. You are not copying a result — you are inheriting a proven shape for the argument. The “How this paper was built” commentary at the end of each paper is the map for doing that translation, and the JSSR-ready 200–300-word abstract is the model your own abstract should match in shape, not in topic.
Know the standard you are graded against. These exemplars are written one level above the required ASSIP deliverable on purpose. The Week-8 capstone rubric grades your poster + JSSR abstract + talk + packet — not a full paper — but every rubric row (identification, robustness, reproducibility, defense, honesty) is sharpened by reading the full narrative the poster compresses from. Read the rubric alongside the matching exemplar and ask, criterion by criterion, where this exemplar would score and why — then hold your own poster panels and abstract to the same bar.
A note for instructors. These five papers double as the instructor’s anchor papers: they are the worked references in IM-5: Answer Keys and Anchor Work, where each is mapped to the rubric and to its source notebook for use in grading calibration and class discussion.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
text:
Abstract
A raw gap in mortgage-denial rates between minority and non-minority applicants mixes two things a regulator cares about keeping apart: differential treatment (the same applicant getting a different answer because of group) and differential composition (groups that genuinely differ in the risk factors a lender is allowed to price). This paper measures how much of the gap is which, using a Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition of a denial outcome on a set of legitimate underwriting controls. On a synthetic, HMDA-like dataset of 60,000 applications built with a known amount of planted discrimination, the raw 43.9-percentage-point denial gap shrinks to a residual of 21.6 points once income, loan-to-value, debt-to-income, and credit score are held fixed: legitimate risk explains about half the raw gap, and a contested residual of roughly equal size survives. We then demonstrate the two failure modes that determine whether that residual can be believed. Omitting the credit score — the one variable real HMDA does not contain — inflates the residual by more than half (to 32.9 points), so any HMDA-only number overstates differential treatment from a missing column, not from malice. Conversely, over-controlling on a post-treatment pricing channel collapses the residual and flips its sign, regressing away the very effect we are hunting. Because the design is a selection-on-observables decomposition, not a natural experiment, we read the residual as a disparity consistent with differential treatment under the assumption that the controls capture all legitimate risk and nothing on the discrimination pathway — an assumption HMDA’s missing score means we cannot defend on real data. The exercise is methodological: it shows what the gap-decomposition can and cannot establish, and why fair-lending work since Sun and Gao (2019) reaches for a research design rather than a longer control list.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 1. Introduction
text:
1. Introduction
In a recent reporting year, applicants from majority-minority neighborhoods were denied mortgages at nearly twice the rate of applicants from majority-white neighborhoods, and the gap narrows but does not vanish once income and loan size are held fixed.1 Whether such a gap reflects differential treatment — lenders applying a different rule to otherwise-similar applicants because of group — or differential composition — groups that genuinely differ in the creditworthiness a lender is legally allowed to price — is simultaneously a live question for fair-lending regulators and an unresolved empirical one. The entire intellectual content of fair lending lives in that distinction, because a raw denial-rate gap confounds the two, and no journalist’s headline number can separate them.
This paper provides a methodological anatomy of that confound: it decomposes the minority–non-minority mortgage-denial gap into the part explained by legitimate, observable risk and the residual that survives, and it shows precisely how two common analytic mistakes — omitting an unobserved risk factor, and over-controlling on a variable that channels the discrimination — move the residual in opposite, equally misleading directions. Our contribution is not a fact about any real lender; it is a worked demonstration, on data whose truth we planted, of what the gap-decomposition design can and cannot establish, and of why the missing credit score in real HMDA forces fair-lending researchers toward a design rather than a longer regression.
We find, on a synthetic HMDA-like dataset of 60,000 applications, that the raw denial gap of 43.9 percentage points shrinks to a residual of 21.6 points once income, loan-to-value (LTV), debt-to-income (DTI), and credit score are held fixed — legitimate risk explains about half the raw gap (22.3 points, 51%), and a contested residual of roughly equal size (21.6 points, 49%) remains. Two manipulations then bound the residual’s fragility. Dropping the credit score, the one variable real HMDA does not carry, inflates the residual by 11.3 points (to 32.9, a 52% increase), because the omitted score is both protective and correlated with group: textbook omitted-variable bias, finally measured rather than feared. Adding a post-treatment pricing variable collapses the residual from 20.9 points to −6.0, reversing its sign — a vivid over-controlling failure. Because the residual rests on selection-on-observables, not on any natural experiment, we read it throughout as a disparity consistent with differential treatment under a strong and untestable assumption, never as a causal estimate of discrimination.
The remainder proceeds as follows. Section 2 positions the exercise in the fair-lending literature. Section 3 describes the synthetic data and how it mimics HMDA. Section 4 lays out the decomposition design and states the identifying assumption explicitly, with a threats table. Section 5 presents the headline decomposition. Section 6 reports the robustness exercises — the omitted-score inflation, the over-controlling collapse, and a race-blind benchmark — organized around the threats to interpretation. Section 7 concludes with the honest limits.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 2. Positioning in the literature
text:
2. Positioning in the literature
Fair-lending empirics divide along two seams this paper sits across. The first is the margin: discrimination can live on the acceptance margin (who gets a loan) or the pricing margin (what they pay conditional on getting one), and a lender can launder a disparity from one to the other — approving everyone but pricing the disfavored group higher, or pricing uniformly but denying more. A complete verdict needs both. Bartlett, Morse, Stanton, and Wallace (2022) work the pricing margin, asking whether minority borrowers pay higher rates conditional on the GSE risk inputs that mechanically determine what a conforming loan “should” cost; Bhutta, Hizmo, and Ringo (2022, 2025) work primarily the acceptance margin, decomposing the raw racial denial gap once they can finally observe the credit score the public record omits. This paper lives on the acceptance margin, and inherits BHR’s central move: watch the group coefficient march across columns as the legitimate controls enter.
The second seam is how identification is achieved, and it defines the whole literature’s difficulty. Because the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act register records who applied, where, for how much, and what happened — but not the applicant’s credit score — a HMDA-only analyst cannot condition on the most important legitimate risk factor, and so cannot tell whether a residual gap is differential treatment or the missing score in disguise. The literature responds in three ways. One strand documents the raw gap descriptively and stops, honest that it cannot separate treatment from composition. A second acquires the missing creditworthiness from outside HMDA — the BHR move — and measures the omitted-variable bias the first could only fear. A third abandons the regression for a research design: Sun and Gao (2019), studying whether same-sex couples were treated differently when they applied to borrow, reached for matched comparison and policy variation precisely because the score was missing and a control list could not carry the argument all the way to a court or a Congressional hearing. Our exercise belongs to the second strand in spirit — we observe the score, because we built it — but its purpose is pedagogical: a ground-truth demonstration of why the residual from a HMDA-only decomposition is neither nothing nor a clean estimate of discrimination, but a bounded and fragile number whose fragility we can see because we planted its truth.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 3. Data
text:
3. Data
We use a synthetic, seeded, loan-level dataset of N = 60{,}000 mortgage applications, generated in nb6.4 with a single pinned random generator (numpy default generator, seed 42) so every number regenerates bit-for-bit. The dataset mimics the shape of an aggregated HMDA extract — a binary denial outcome, a protected-group indicator, and underwriting risk factors — while differing from real HMDA in the one respect that makes it useful for instruction: we know the data-generating process, so we know the true amount of discrimination it contains.
Each application carries a protected-group indicator, minority \in \{0,1\} (a 50% share, by construction), and four legitimate risk factors a fair lender is allowed to use: annual income (in $000s), the loan-to-value ratio (LTV, in percent), the debt-to-income ratio (DTI, in percent), and a FICO-like credit score (300–850, higher is safer). Two construction choices are load-bearing and disclosed in full, because the honesty of a synthetic study lives entirely in its data-generating process. First, the risk factors genuinely differ across groups for reasons upstream of the lender: the minority group has, on average, modestly lower income and credit scores and higher LTV and DTI, reflecting the kind of wealth-and-credit-access gaps a non-discriminating lender would nonetheless price. This is real, legitimate risk, and it is exactly what makes the raw gap an unreliable measure of discrimination. We do not assert these upstream patterns are fair — a credit score shaped by historical inequity is itself contestable (Section 7) — only that a lender applying them identically across groups would still produce a raw gap. Second, the denial decision is a latent risk index plus a tunable direct-discrimination penalty applied to minority applicants for no risk reason at all: pure differential treatment, set to a known nonzero value, with denial recorded when the index crosses a threshold. The dataset also carries an offered interest rate, set downstream of the index and carrying its own group markup — a variable we deliberately misuse in Section 6 to demonstrate over-controlling.
The overall denial rate is 0.478; the minority group’s rate is 0.697 against the non-minority group’s 0.258, the 43.9-point raw gap the rest of the paper takes apart. The single most important way this dataset is unlike the world it imitates is also the lesson of the whole literature: in real HMDA the credit score is not observed. We observe it here only because we built it, and Section 6 uses that artificial visibility to measure exactly what its real-world absence costs.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 4. Empirical design and identification
text:
4. Empirical design and identification
The specification. We estimate a linear probability model (LPM) of denial on the protected-group indicator and a build-up of legitimate risk controls, using the LPM rather than a logit because its coefficients are differences in probabilities readable directly in percentage points — the currency a fair-lending decomposition trades in. Writing D_i for denial of application i, M_i for the minority indicator, and \mathbf{X}_i for the risk controls (income, LTV, DTI, score),

D_i = \beta_0 + \beta\, M_i + \boldsymbol{\delta}'\mathbf{X}_i + \varepsilon_i,

the coefficient \beta, scaled to percentage points, is the residual denial gap: the share of the raw gap surviving after the controls are held fixed. We complement the column build-up with a Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition (Blinder, 1973; Oaxaca, 1973), which splits the raw mean gap into an explained part (groups differ in \mathbf{X}, priced by the non-minority rule) and an unexplained residual (the same \mathbf{X} priced differently across groups) as an exact accounting identity. We use the non-minority coefficients as the non-discriminatory benchmark — the standard index choice — and note the qualitative split is robust to the well-known index-number ambiguity.
The spec, named in full (CONVENTIONS §4). Outcome = loan denial (0/1), read in percentage points. Key regressor = the minority indicator. Controls = income, LTV, DTI, credit score, entered as a build-up. Fixed effects = none (a single cross-section). Clustering = none; we report classical and heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, because this is a measurement exercise on i.i.d. synthetic draws, not a panel-inference showdown — there is no repeated unit to cluster on, and Section 6 confirms the choice does not move the verdict. Sample = all 60,000 synthetic applications, held fixed across every column.
The identifying assumption, in one sentence. The residual coefficient \beta equals differential treatment only if the controls \mathbf{X} capture all of the legitimate risk a lender is allowed to price, and contain nothing that lies on the discrimination pathway. This is a selection-on-observables assumption, and it is strong — not a natural-experiment assumption: there is no policy shock, no parallel-trends bet, no instrument. Identification rests entirely on the conditioning set, which is why the literature’s first question is always “what is in the controls, and is the score in there?” The assumption has two distinct failure directions, and naming both is the discipline this design demands.
Threats to interpretation. Table 2 states the threats and responses in descending order of danger. The most dangerous — an omitted legitimate risk factor, namely the credit score real HMDA lacks — is the one a regulator asks about first, and the one Section 6 measures directly.
Table 2 — Threats to the interpretation of the residual gap, and responses









Threat
Why it is plausible here
What we do about it
Residual concern




Omitted creditworthiness (a legitimate risk factor we cannot see)
Real HMDA omits the credit score; the score is protective and lower in the minority group, so leaving it out dumps real risk into the residual and inflates apparent discrimination (classic OVB).
Section 6.1: drop the score and measure the inflation against the full-information residual; report both.
On real HMDA the score is gone — we can only bound, not eliminate, this bias; soft information a human underwriter sees is never in any file.


Over-controlling on the discrimination pathway (a post-treatment mediator)
The offered rate is set downstream of the decision and carries a group markup; “holding loan terms fixed” would absorb part of the very effect we hunt.
Section 6.2: add the offered rate on purpose and show the residual collapse and flip sign — a demonstration of why “more controls” is not “better controls.”
Judging which controls are confounders vs. channels requires institutional knowledge a dataset cannot supply.


Functional form (LPM approximating a nonlinear threshold rule)
The true rule is a nonlinear threshold; the LPM is a linear approximation, so a small residual can be approximation error, not discrimination.
Section 6.3: the race-blind benchmark drives the residual to ~1.3 pp, locating the LPM’s approximation error and confirming it is tiny next to the human residual.
The LPM is read for interpretability, not efficiency; magnitudes near zero should be read as “indistinguishable from no differential treatment,” not exactly zero.


Definition of “discrimination” (disparate treatment vs. disparate impact)
A race-blind rule that uses a score shaped by historical inequity can produce disparate impact even with zero disparate treatment.
Section 7: state which legal definition each number speaks to before quoting it.
Conditioning on the score may control away a channel of disparate impact; this design speaks to treatment, not impact.



The residual-concern column is substantive in every row, which is the point: this is an observational decomposition, and a row with a blank residual would be a tell, not a triumph.

Sample: 60,000 synthetic, HMDA-like applications from nb6.4 (seed 42), held fixed across all columns. Estimator: linear probability model (OLS on a binary outcome). Controls enter as a build-up from the raw bivariate gap (1) to the full legitimate-risk set (4); the score enters only in (4). Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors in parentheses; classical standard errors are nearly identical (Section 6.3) and do not move the stars. *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.10. All figures are illustrative outputs of a synthetic dataset, not empirical estimates.
Read the minority coefficient leftward across the columns — 43.9 \to 39.8 \to 32.4 \to 20.9 — and the table tells its story without the prose. The raw gap of 43.9 percentage points is large and alarming, exactly the number a headline would quote. Income alone explains about four points; LTV and DTI carry the gap to 32.4; and the credit score, entering last in column (4), is the single most consequential control, pulling the residual to 20.9 points. The sample size is constant at 60,000 across every column, so the shrinkage reflects the controls doing their work, not a silently changing sample — the march is about composition, not selection. Every coefficient is precisely estimated (HC1 standard errors near 0.3–0.4 points, all three-starred), but precision is not importance: the point is the movement, which says roughly half the raw association was legitimate risk masquerading as a gap.
The Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition states that movement as an accounting identity. Of the 43.9-point raw gap, 22.3 points (51%) are explained by group differences in the legitimate risk factors — the minority group’s higher LTV and DTI and lower income and score, priced by the non-minority group’s own rule — and 21.6 points (49%) are the unexplained residual, the share that would survive if the two groups had identical risk profiles but were scored by different rules. The two parts sum to the raw gap by construction. The 21.6-point residual is our measured differential treatment within this dataset and under the Section 4 assumption. Because we planted a known discrimination penalty in the data-generating process, we can say what no analyst of real HMDA ever can: the decomposition recovered a residual in the right neighborhood of the truth we built, which is what licenses trusting the method — not any number — when it is later pointed at data whose truth cannot be seen.
A note on language, because the design caps it. This is a selection-on-observables decomposition, not a randomized or quasi-experiment. The honest verb is “is associated with,” the honest object “a residual disparity,” never “discrimination causes the gap.” The 21.6-point residual is a disparity consistent with differential treatment under the assumption that the controls capture all legitimate risk and nothing on the discrimination pathway — the hedge placed on the assumption, not smeared across the claim. Section 6 shows how much that hedge is doing.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 6. Robustness
text:
6. Robustness
The robustness exercises mirror Table 2’s threats, in the same order of danger. Each states what a pass (or a failure) would look like before reporting the result. Note the distinction the section keeps visible throughout: §6.1 and §6.2 are tests of the design’s interpretation (do the controls satisfy the identifying assumption?), while §6.3 is a stability check on functional form. None of them can rescue the design from its central limitation — that on real HMDA the credit score is unobservable — and we say so plainly.

6.1 The omitted-creditworthiness threat: drop the score and measure the bias
A reader’s first and most dangerous worry is that the residual is contaminated by a legitimate risk factor we cannot see — and on real HMDA the missing factor is named: the credit score. The prediction this design makes is sharp. The score is protective (higher score, lower denial) and lower in the minority group, so both conditions for omitted-variable bias hold, and the direction is the dangerous one: omitting the score dumps real risk into the residual and inflates apparent discrimination. A pass for the worry would be a residual that barely moves when the score is removed; an honest confirmation of the threat is a residual that jumps.
It jumps. Re-running the decomposition with the score omitted — simulating a HMDA-only analyst — moves the unexplained residual from 21.6 points (score in) to 32.9 points (score out), an inflation of 11.3 points, or 52%. Same data, same planted truth; one missing column moves the verdict by more than half. This is Week-2 omitted-variable bias made concrete and measured rather than feared, and it is the empirical heart of why a HMDA-only residual cannot be read as discrimination: a real analyst, lacking the score through no fault of their own, would overstate differential treatment substantially. The concern does not close — on real data the score is gone, and even the richest outside-HMDA file omits the soft information a human underwriter weighs — so our 21.6-point residual is best read as the least inflated estimate this dataset can produce, with real-world numbers necessarily worse.


6.2 The over-controlling threat: add a mediator and watch the sign flip
The mirror-image worry is that “more controls” silently becomes “wrong controls.” The offered interest rate is set downstream of the denial decision and carries its own group markup — a post-treatment mediator that channels part of the discrimination. A naive analyst reaching for rigor might add it to “hold loan terms fixed.” The prediction: conditioning on a variable on the discrimination pathway absorbs the very effect we estimate, so the residual should collapse — a failure of the analyst, not of the design.
It collapses and reverses. Adding the offered rate to the full-control specification moves the minority residual from 20.9 points to −6.0 points — not merely shrunk but sign-flipped to a nonsensical “minority applicants are denied less” artifact. The discrimination did not disappear; we controlled it away, because part of the planted bias flows through the rate markup and conditioning on the mediator soaks it up. The operative question for every control is the one a dataset cannot answer on its own: is this variable a confounder to hold fixed, or a channel to leave alone? The residual concern is that judging confounder-versus-channel requires institutional knowledge — which products are “steered,” which fields encode prior decisions — that lives outside any data file.


6.3 The functional-form threat: a race-blind benchmark, and standard-error flavors
Two stability checks. First, because the true decision rule is a nonlinear threshold and the LPM is a linear approximation, a small residual could be approximation error rather than differential treatment. We benchmark against a race-blind rule: re-decide every application using a latent index built from the risk factors only, with the discrimination term forced to zero and the noise draw held fixed, so the only difference from the human rule is whether the group penalty is switched on — the synthetic analogue of BHR’s race-blind automated underwriting system. The race-blind rule drives the residual (after full controls) from the human rule’s 21.0 points to 1.3 points. The residual under a rule that cannot see group is small but not exactly zero, and that ~1.3-point floor is not hidden discrimination — it is the LPM approximating a nonlinear threshold on two groups with different risk distributions. Locating that floor is the point: it is tiny next to the human residual, so the 21.6-point Section 5 residual is overwhelmingly planted treatment, not functional-form artifact. (The raw gap under the race-blind rule falls only to about 26 points, not to zero, because legitimate risk still differs across groups — removing the human removes the discretion channel, not the underlying composition difference.)
Second, the standard-error flavor. The classical homoskedastic standard errors are nearly identical to the HC1 errors of Table 3 (both near 0.3 points on the key coefficient), and neither moves a single star. Pass: the conclusion is invariant to the inference choice, as it should be in a 60,000-observation i.i.d. cross-section with no panel structure to cluster on. This is the one robustness result purely about inference rather than identification, and we flag it as such: it shows the number is not an artifact of an arbitrary SE choice, and says nothing about whether the design is valid. Robustness is not identification.

title: Capstone 1 (Exemplar) — Fair Lending on HMDA: How Much of the Mortgage-Denial Gap Survives the Controls?
section: 7. Conclusion
text:
7. Conclusion
We set out to measure how much of a mortgage-denial gap is legitimate risk and how much is a residual that looks like differential treatment, and to show what determines whether that residual can be believed. On a synthetic, HMDA-like dataset with a known planted disparity, a raw denial gap of 43.9 percentage points decomposes into roughly equal halves: about 22 points explained by group differences in legitimate, observable risk, and a contested residual of about 22 points that survives the full control set. The residual is associated with being in the minority group conditional on observables; under our selection-on-observables assumption it is consistent with differential treatment, and we claim nothing stronger, because the design supports nothing stronger.
The honest limits are the spine of the paper, not an afterthought. First and most important, on real HMDA the credit score is unobservable, and Section 6.1 measured what that costs: omitting the score inflates the residual by more than half. Our 21.6-point residual is an artifact of artificial full information that real data never grants; a real analyst’s number would be worse, and bounded above, not estimated. Second, the residual is a disparate-treatment quantity — a different rule applied to the same inputs — and says little about disparate impact, the distinct legal concern that a facially neutral rule (even a race-blind algorithm) can produce unlawful outcomes if it prices on a score shaped by historical inequity. Conditioning on the credit score may be holding fixed a legitimate risk factor, or controlling away a channel of disparate impact; this design cannot tell, and the policy verdict turns on which it is. Third, the design is a decomposition, not a natural experiment: with no policy shock to lean on, it cannot rule out an unobserved confounder more subtly than by the demonstrations above.
That last limit is the bridge to the rest of the fair-lending track. The reason Sun and Gao (2019) studied lending to same-sex borrowers with a research design — matched comparison and policy variation — rather than a longer control list is exactly the limit we hit: when the decisive risk variable is unobservable, no decomposition can separate treatment from composition, and credibility has to come from the design instead. The natural next step, the one Lab 4 rehearses, is to pair a disparity like this with a clean identification strategy — a staggered state fair-lending policy shock estimated against never-treated controls — so that the parallel-trends assumption, not the impossible “we controlled for everything,” carries the causal weight. This paper is the negative space that motivates that move: a demonstration of how far the decomposition gets, and the precise point at which it cannot go further.

section: How This Paper Was Built — Annotated Margin Commentary
text:
How This Paper Was Built — Annotated Margin Commentary
This section is not part of the paper. It is the exemplar’s teaching layer: a walk through the choices that made the paper above survive a Week-5-style hostile reading, keyed to CONVENTIONS and Appendix D. Read it after the paper, the way you would read a director’s commentary.
Why a decomposition, not the Lab-4 DiD. The capstone track offers two designs. Lab 4 builds a clean staggered difference-in-differences on a HMDA-shaped panel, where a policy shock and never-treated controls let parallel trends carry causal weight. This paper deliberately does the other thing — a cross-sectional Blinder–Oaxaca decomposition (the nb6.4 exercise) — because the two designs license very different verbs, and showing the weaker design done honestly is the more instructive exemplar. A decomposition is selection-on-observables: it can only ever say “associated with,” and the whole craft is refusing to let that creep up to “causes.” If you write the DiD version, your verbs go up a notch (to “causally estimate, under parallel trends”), but the structure, table craft, and limits-paragraph discipline transfer wholesale.
The synthetic-data label is the first and most repeated move. CONVENTIONS §6 forbids fabricating empirical claims, and presenting synthetic numbers as real findings would be exactly that. So the synthetic nature is declared three times, at descending scope: a blockquote banner before the title, a footnote on the first numeric sentence of the introduction, and an italic clause in the Table 3 note. A reader who lands on any entry point — abstract, intro, or headline table — must learn within one screen that the numbers are illustrative. This is not over-hedging; it is the one honest caveat the whole document needs, placed where it cannot be missed.
Every number traces to nb6.4, frozen. Appendix D.2’s last commandment is “generate, don’t retype.” The figures here — 43.9 raw, the 39.8/32.4/20.9 march, the 22.3/21.6 Oaxaca split, the 32.9 omitted-score inflation, the −6.0 over-control flip, the 1.3 race-blind residual — were read off a re-run of the nb6.4 data-generating process at seed 42, not invented to sound plausible. A retyped table drifts from its source; a generated one cannot. For your own paper the tables come out of nb8.3, and you never touch the digits by hand.
The identifying assumption is one sentence, and it states the failure direction. CONVENTIONS §4 demands outcome · treatment · controls · FE · clustering · sample · identifying assumption, and Section 4 names all seven, with the assumption italicized: the residual equals differential treatment only if the controls capture all legitimate risk and nothing on the discrimination pathway. Notice it names both ways the assumption fails — too few controls (omitted score) and the wrong controls (the mediator) — because those become Sections 6.1 and 6.2. A design section that said “we control for confounders” instead would have thrown away the paper’s credibility; D.5.6 bans “controls for endogeneity” for the same reason.
The threats table (Table 2) is ordered by danger and has no blank residuals. Per D.3, the robustness section is organized around the threats table, not around a list of regressions, and the rows descend from the most dangerous threat (the missing score, the thing a regulator asks about first) downward. The residual-concern column is substantive in every row — D.3 is explicit that a blank residual is “a tell, not a triumph.” Section 6 then cashes each row: §6.1 answers the omitted-score row, §6.2 the over-control row, §6.3 the functional-form row, each opening by stating what a pass looks like before reporting the result, so there is no freedom to redefine “pass” after seeing the number.
Table 3 is built to the D.1/D.2 standard, and to stand alone. Columns are specifications built parsimonious-to-saturated (raw → +income → +income,LTV,DTI → +all incl. score), not variables; the key coefficient sits on top in every column with its standard error beneath; controls collapse into Yes/No switch rows rather than spraying nuisance coefficients; N is on every column and constant at 60,000, defusing the silent-sample-change trap; stars are defined; the SE flavor (HC1) is named. Two deliberate departures from the D.1 worked example: there are no fixed effects (a single cross-section), so the table reports ordinary R^2, not within-R^2 — D.2 §2’s rule is “within-R^2 for FE models,” and using it here would be wrong. And there is no clustering: with 60,000 i.i.d. draws and no repeated unit, there is nothing to cluster on, so the note says HC1 and §6.3 confirms classical SEs agree. Reporting clustered SEs to look sophisticated would have been a craft error; the honest move is to say why clustering does not apply.
The verbs are audited against the weakest assumption (D.5.1). Run the D.5 verb-audit on the paper and every verb attached to the residual is “associated with,” “consistent with,” “a residual disparity,” “survives” — never “causes,” “leads to,” or “discriminates against.” The abstract, intro preview, results, and conclusion are held to the same ceiling to prevent the drift D.5.2 warns about, where the abstract hedges and the conclusion overclaims. The single hedge is placed on the assumption (“under the assumption that the controls capture all legitimate risk”), not smeared across every sentence as mush. The contribution sentence (D.5.3) states what is now known (a worked demonstration of what the decomposition can and cannot establish), not what we did, and its verb is calibrated to a methodological exercise, not a discovery.
Citations are real and load-bearing (D.5.4, CONVENTIONS §6). Sun and Gao (2019) is cited exactly per the camp’s anchor list and used to position — it marks the wall of the map (why the field reaches for design) and the edge of our gap (where the decomposition stops). Bartlett et al. and BHR set up the pricing-vs-acceptance and human-vs-algorithm seams; Blinder and Oaxaca are the method’s primary sources, cited because the paper uses their decomposition by name, not to pad. The one [CHECK] in the references is honest and deliberate: a real paper must pin the HMDA vintage, and since this exemplar uses no real HMDA figure, it flags the obligation rather than inventing a snapshot date — exactly the “tag the hole, never fabricate” rule.
The honest-limits paragraph is the spine, not the footnote (D.5.5). Section 7 leads its limits with the single most damaging one — the unobservable score on real HMDA — and states the disparate-treatment-vs-disparate-impact distinction that determines the policy verdict, then bridges to the DiD design as the way past the limit. This is the conceded-fatal-critique move: naming your own worst vulnerability before a referee does is what makes the rest of the paper trustworthy. The conclusion resists the verb-creep D.5.5 warns of — no “proves,” no “establishes” — and ends by pointing forward to the cleaner design rather than declaring the question settled.
What a student should copy, and what they should not. Copy the structure (the seven-section skeleton, the four-move intro, the threats table cashed out as the robustness section), the table craft, the verb discipline, and above all the limits paragraph. Do not copy the numbers — they are synthetic — and do not copy the “no clustering” choice into a panel paper, where it would be the BDM disease. The exemplar’s deepest lesson is the one Lab 4 and Mentor 4 drilled: a disparity is not a finding, the residual from a control list is neither nothing nor a clean causal effect, and the credibility of a fair-lending paper comes from the design and the honesty about its limits, never from the length of the control list.

title: Capstone 2 (Exemplar) — Common Ownership from 13F
text:
Common Ownership and Voluntary Disclosure: Evidence from a Synthetic 13F Panel
A capstone exemplar by “Maya R.” (ASSIP 2026 (Aspiring Scientists Summer Internship Program), Cohort 2026), advised by Prof. Lei Gao

title: Capstone 2 (Exemplar) — Common Ownership from 13F
text:
Abstract
When the same large institutional investors hold big stakes in two different firms, those firms are said to be under common ownership — and a growing literature argues this shared ownership changes how firms behave toward one another. I build a firm-pair common-ownership measure from quarterly 13F institutional holdings and relate it to a firm’s voluntary disclosure, the forward-looking guidance a firm chooses to release. On a synthetic 13F-like panel of 600 firms over 24 quarters (2018Q1–2023Q4), built to mimic the structure of the real data, I estimate panel fixed-effects regressions of a disclosure index on a firm’s average common ownership with its product-market peers. In the saturated specification — firm and quarter fixed effects, standard errors clustered by firm — a one-standard-deviation increase in common ownership is associated with a 0.18-point higher disclosure index (about 11% of a standard deviation), and the association is stable across the build-up of controls. These magnitudes are illustrative outputs of synthetic data, not estimates of any real-world effect. I treat the result as observational throughout: common ownership is not randomly assigned, and I devote the design and robustness sections to the threats that follow from that fact. The exercise mirrors, in miniature and on instructional data, the structural question Gao, Han, Kim & Pan (2024) ask of real supply-chain overlapping institutional ownership and supplier-firm earnings management — same identifying frame, different sensor on the outcome (see the student-track variant notice above).



1. Introduction
In a typical recent quarter, the three largest U.S. asset managers together held more than 5% of almost every company in the S&P 500, and often far more — the same handful of institutions sitting on the share registers of firms that compete with one another in the same product market. That fact, a curiosity two decades ago, is now the center of an active debate in finance, antitrust, and corporate governance: when the same owners hold competing firms, do those firms still behave as rivals? The answer bears on the prices consumers pay, on how aggressively firms innovate, and — the angle this paper takes — on how much firms voluntarily tell the market. The overlap itself is easy to document from public filings; what is hard, and contested, is whether it changes firm behavior or merely reflects something else about which firms attract the same investors.
This paper constructs a firm-pair common-ownership measure from 13F institutional holdings and relates it to firm-level voluntary disclosure, asking whether firms more commonly owned with their product-market peers disclose differently. The contribution is to document, on a transparent and reproducible 13F-based measure, a robust panel association between common ownership and voluntary disclosure — and to be honest about why that association is an association and not yet a causal effect. I deliberately do not claim to estimate a causal effect, because, as Section 4 argues, common ownership is endogenous: investors choose which firms to co-hold, and the same forces that draw them to co-hold two firms may independently drive those firms’ disclosure.
I find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s average common ownership with its peers is associated with a 0.18-point increase in its disclosure index — roughly 11% of the index’s standard deviation — in the most demanding specification, which absorbs firm and quarter fixed effects and clusters by firm. The association moves only modestly as I add controls and fixed effects (from 0.24 in the bivariate column to 0.18 in the saturated one): about a quarter of the raw correlation is confounding the controls and fixed effects soak up, and the rest survives the most demanding specification I can run on observational data. The association is robust to alternative clustering, an alternative ownership measure, and dropping the largest investors; it does not survive as a clean causal claim, and I say so. All of these numbers are computed on synthetic data and are illustrative only.
The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 positions the exercise in the common-ownership literature. Section 3 describes the synthetic 13F panel and how the common-ownership measure is built from holdings overlap. Section 4 lays out the panel specification, states the identifying assumption in one sentence, and confronts the endogeneity of ownership in a threats table. Section 5 presents the headline results. Section 6 reports robustness organized around the threats. Section 7 concludes with the limits the design cannot escape.


2. Positioning in the literature
Three strands of work meet at the question this paper asks, and the gap I occupy is visible only once they are placed side by side rather than listed.
The first strand measures common ownership and documents its rise. From the observation that index funds and large active managers hold diversified stakes across whole industries, this literature built the standard tools for quantifying overlap — pairwise co-holding, portfolio-weighted measures of how much two firms’ investors coincide — and showed overlap has grown dramatically. It tells us common ownership is large; it does not tell us what it does. The second strand asks what overlap does to product-market competition, and it is where the controversy lives: one line argues commonly owned firms compete less aggressively and raise prices, while subsequent papers contest both the measurement and the identification, arguing the correlations may reflect which industries attract diversified investors rather than a causal softening of competition. The unresolved core of that debate is exactly the endogeneity problem this paper foregrounds — ownership is chosen, not assigned, so a raw correlation between overlap and any outcome is suspect until the design says otherwise.
The third strand — the one this paper sits closest to — connects common ownership to firm-level reporting and information behavior. The anchor is Gao, Han, Kim & Pan (2024), who study overlapping institutional ownership along the supply chain — the same institutions holding large stakes in both a supplier and its customer — and relate it to the earnings management of the supplier firms, measured as discretionary accruals (the slack with which managers shape the reported earnings number away from the underlying cash reality). Their setting is the supplier–customer link with earnings management as the outcome; mine is the product-market peer with voluntary disclosure as a sibling outcome — a simpler construct for the camp to build, but driven by the same economic mechanism. The conceptual move is the same: an investor who holds both sides of a relationship internalizes information spillovers between them, which can change how the firm both reports its results and talks about them. Where Gao, Han, Kim & Pan (2024) bring a careful identification strategy and an accruals-based outcome to the supply-chain case, this exemplar is more modest, runs on a different but related outcome (voluntary disclosure), and is honest about its limits — it documents the panel association on a transparent 13F measure and stops short of the causal claim. The gap I fill is therefore not a gap in the real literature; it is a pedagogical one: a fully worked, reproducible, synthetic-data example of how to build the measure, run the panel, and report it to the Appendix-D standard, with the causal language disciplined to what an observational design can bear.


3. Data

3.1 The 13F source and what it does and does not tell us
The raw ingredient of any common-ownership measure is Form 13F, the quarterly report that institutional investment managers with over $100 million in qualifying U.S. equity assets must file with the SEC, disclosing their long equity positions — which stocks, how many shares, what market value — as of each calendar quarter-end. There are two routes to it: the free, public SEC EDGAR filings (the exact information-table XML, which you de-duplicate and clean yourself), and the licensed, cleaned Thomson Reuters / Refinitiv s34 panel on WRDS (de-duplicated, consistent manager identifiers, but bound by the GMU-infrastructure rule). For a real version of this project the choice between them is the whole methodological point; for this exemplar I use neither, because the data are synthetic — but the synthetic panel mirrors the EDGAR information-table schema (one row per manager-quarter-holding: manager id, CUSIP, period, shares, value) so the measure-building code would run unchanged on a real EDGAR pull.
Three limits of 13F are conceptual constraints the design must respect, because they bound what any common-ownership measure can mean. First, 13F reports long positions only — no shorts, no most derivatives — so disclosed holdings are not a manager’s true net exposure; a “common owner” measured from 13F is a common long owner. Second, the 45-day reporting lag makes holdings stale by the time they are filed, so a 13F-based measure is a lagged snapshot, never real-time positioning. Third, the “who is one manager” problem — family-of-funds and sub-advisor structures mean the same assets can appear under several filer identities, so the measure is sensitive to how managers are aggregated, a modeling choice I state rather than a data field I read. (A fourth caveat, CUSIP licensing, is a publishing constraint: CUSIPs may be used inside an analysis but a CUSIP master file may not be redistributed; my synthetic data sidesteps this by inventing identifiers.)


3.2 Building the common-ownership measure from holdings overlap
The construct begins with a single intuition stated in one sentence: two firms are commonly owned to the degree that the same institutions hold large stakes in both. Turning that sentence into a number takes three steps, and I show the arithmetic on a tiny example before the formula, because a number before a Greek letter is the camp’s rule.
Step one — ownership shares. For each firm j and quarter t, and each institution m, compute the fraction of firm j’s shares outstanding that manager m holds, call it w_{mjt}. If BlackRock holds 7% of Firm A and 5% of Firm B, then w_{\text{BlackRock},A,t}=0.07 and w_{\text{BlackRock},B,t}=0.05.
Step two — pairwise overlap. For a pair of firms (j,k), sum across institutions the product of the two ownership shares:

\text{CO}_{jkt} \;=\; \sum_{m} w_{mjt}\, w_{mkt}.

This is large when the same managers hold large stakes in both firms, and zero when no institution holds both. In the toy example, if BlackRock is the only common holder the pair’s overlap is 0.07 \times 0.05 = 0.0035; add Vanguard at 6% and 6% and it grows by 0.06\times0.06 = 0.0036, to 0.0071. The measure rewards both how many institutions co-hold and how large their stakes are — the portfolio-weighted spirit of the standard common-ownership measures, simplified to what 13F shares-outstanding ratios support.
Step three — aggregate to the firm. A firm’s exposure to common ownership is its average overlap with its product-market peers. Let \mathcal{P}_j be the set of firm j’s peers (in the synthetic data, firms in the same of 30 simulated industries); then

\text{CommonOwn}_{jt} \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_j|}\sum_{k \in \mathcal{P}_j} \text{CO}_{jkt}.

This firm-quarter number is the key regressor. I standardize it (mean zero, unit variance within the sample) so that coefficients read in standard-deviation units, which the Appendix-D craft prefers to raw magnitudes that would print as 0.0003.


3.3 The synthetic panel and the outcome
The panel is 600 firms across 24 quarters (2018Q1–2023Q4), N = 14{,}400 firm-quarters, partitioned into 30 industries of 20 firms each. Holdings are simulated for 200 institutions whose choices induce realistic overlap: large “index-like” managers hold broad, correlated baskets (generating high common ownership), while smaller managers hold concentrated, idiosyncratic positions. The outcome, \text{Disclosure}_{jt}, is a synthetic voluntary-disclosure index — a standardized count of forward-looking guidance items a firm issued that quarter (a sibling outcome to the supplier-firm earnings management Gao, Han, Kim & Pan (2024) study; see the student-track variant notice at the top) — built to carry a modest positive association with common ownership plus firm-level persistence, an industry-time component, and substantial noise, so the estimation problem is non-trivial and the fixed effects do real work. Because I built the data-generating process, I know the “true” association I planted — exactly why this is a teaching exemplar and not evidence. Controls (log assets, leverage, a profitability proxy) are simulated to correlate with both ownership and disclosure, so omitting them would bias the bivariate estimate and the build-up across columns is informative.

All values are illustrative.



4. Empirical design and identification

4.1 Specification
I estimate a two-way fixed-effects panel regression of disclosure on lagged common ownership:

\text{Disclosure}_{jt} \;=\; \beta\,\text{CommonOwn}_{j,t-1} \;+\; \boldsymbol{\delta}'\mathbf{X}_{j,t-1} \;+\; \alpha_j \;+\; \lambda_t \;+\; \varepsilon_{jt},

stated in the CONVENTIONS §4 form so every slot is explicit:

Outcome: \text{Disclosure}_{jt}, the firm-quarter voluntary-disclosure index (synthetic).
Key regressor: \text{CommonOwn}_{j,t-1}, the firm’s standardized average common ownership with its product-market peers, lagged one quarter to respect the 45-day 13F reporting lag and to reduce the most mechanical reverse-causality channel.
Controls \mathbf{X}: log assets, leverage, profitability, all lagged.
Fixed effects: firm fixed effects \alpha_j (absorbing everything time-invariant about a firm — its business model, its baseline disclosure culture) and quarter fixed effects \lambda_t (absorbing market-wide shocks to disclosure, such as a regulatory change or a recession quarter).
Clustering: standard errors clustered by firm (600 clusters), the level at which residuals are most obviously correlated.
Sample: the synthetic panel, 600 firms × 24 quarters, N = 14{,}400 firm-quarters (the lag costs the first quarter, leaving 13,800 in estimation; reported below).
Identifying assumption (one sentence): conditional on firm and quarter fixed effects and the controls, within-firm changes in lagged common ownership are uncorrelated with within-firm shocks to disclosure — that is, the timing of changes in who co-holds a firm is, after the fixed effects, as good as unrelated to the firm’s disclosure shocks.

I want to be plain about that assumption: I do not believe it holds cleanly, and the design does not let me test it directly — which is why every causal verb is absent from this paper. The firm fixed effects buy that I am not comparing high- to low-common-ownership firms (a comparison hopelessly confounded by what kind of firm attracts diversified investors); I am comparing a firm to itself as its common ownership changes. The quarter fixed effects buy that a market-wide swing in disclosure or institutional flows does not masquerade as a common-ownership effect. What neither buys is protection against a time-varying, firm-specific confounder — a firm becoming more transparent for its own reasons and, for the same reasons, more attractive to the big diversified funds.


4.2 Why clustering is not optional here (recall Petersen)
This is a panel: the same 600 firms over 24 quarters. The lesson of Petersen (2009) is that on such data, residuals for the same firm across quarters are correlated — a firm that discloses a lot this quarter tends to next quarter too — so classical or heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors that ignore this within-firm correlation are too small, inflating t-statistics and manufacturing false significance (the Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan disease). The defensible default is to cluster by firm, the level at which the dependence is strongest and at which the key regressor varies most. I report firm-clustered errors throughout and, in Section 6, show what happens under two-way (firm and quarter) and industry clustering — because the clustering choice, not the point estimate, is where a Week-5-trained referee looks first.


4.3 Threats to identification
Common ownership is endogenous, full stop. The honest way to present that is the threats-and-responses table, in descending order of danger. Column 3 reports what I actually do; column 4 is the residual concern that survives, and it is the column a mentor reads first.
Table 2 — Threats to identification and responses









Threat
Why it’s plausible here
What I do about it
Residual concern




Time-varying firm-level confounder (selection on a firm trend)
A firm becoming more transparent for its own reasons may simultaneously attract diversified institutions, so within-firm co-movement of ownership and disclosure is not the ownership causing disclosure.
Firm FE remove fixed firm traits; I add lagged controls and (§6) a firm-specific linear trend.
A firm trend that is non-linear or coincident with the ownership change is not absorbed; this is the threat the design cannot kill, and it caps my verbs at “associated with.”


Reverse causality (disclosure drives ownership)
Funds may buy firms because they disclose more (transparency lowers monitoring cost), so the arrow could run outcome → regressor.
I lag common ownership one quarter (also matching the 45-day 13F lag) and, in §6, lag it two quarters.
Lagging reduces but does not eliminate reverse causality if funds anticipate future disclosure.


Measurement / manager-aggregation error
The “who is one manager” problem: family-of-funds structures mean the same assets appear under several filers, so CO is mismeasured, biasing \hat\beta (classically, toward zero).
§6 rebuilds CO with an alternative measure (count of common holders above a 1% stake) and drops the five largest managers.
Attenuation from remaining mismeasurement means my estimate is, if anything, a lower bound — but I cannot sign every component of the error.


Industry-time shocks (a peer-group story)
An industry-wide event could move both peers’ ownership and a firm’s disclosure together within a quarter, beyond what quarter FE absorb.
§6 adds industry × quarter fixed effects.
Sub-industry shocks finer than my 30-industry partition remain.



The table makes the paper’s stance explicit. There is no row whose residual concern is “none,” because every observational design on chosen ownership has leftover doubt, and a blank fourth column would be a tell that I had not looked hard enough. The most dangerous row — the time-varying firm-level confounder — is the one the fixed effects cannot dispatch, and it is the reason this paper documents an association rather than estimating an effect.



5. Results

The key regressor is the firm’s average common ownership with its product-market peers, lagged one quarter and standardized to unit variance, so the coefficient is the change in the disclosure index per one-standard-deviation increase in common ownership. Column (1) and (2) report the ordinary R^2; column (3) reports the within-R^2. *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.10.
The headline coefficient is 0.18 in the saturated column (3): a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s lagged common ownership with its peers is associated with a 0.18-point higher disclosure index. Since the disclosure index has a standard deviation of 1.62, that is about 0.18/1.62 \approx 11\% of a standard deviation — a modest but not trivial association in human terms, the kind of magnitude one would want to weigh against the cost of the disclosure it represents, not just note as statistically distinguishable from zero. The estimate carries two stars: with a firm-clustered standard error of 0.061, the t-statistic is 0.18/0.061 \approx 3.0, which a reader can confirm from the table without trusting my prose.
The story across the columns is the one the build-up is designed to tell. The raw bivariate association is 0.24; adding the firm characteristics that correlate with both ownership and disclosure pulls it to 0.21; absorbing firm and quarter fixed effects pulls it to 0.18. The coefficient shrinks by about a quarter from raw to saturated and then holds rather than collapsing toward zero. The honest reading: some of the raw correlation was confounding (bigger, more profitable firms both attract diversified owners and disclose more, which the controls and firm FE remove), but a stable association remains within firms once the obvious confounders are absorbed. That stability speaks to the robustness of the number; it is silent about whether the number is causal, the distinction Section 6 keeps in view.
The bottom block is the reality check. N is constant at 13,800 across all three columns because no control is ever missing, so the leftward shrinkage reflects the added controls and fixed effects, not a quietly changing sample. The fit row reports the ordinary R^2 for the no-FE columns and the within-R^2 for column (3), labeled as such: the within-R^2 of 0.034 says that after the firm and quarter intercepts absorb the large between-firm and between-quarter variation, common ownership and the controls explain about 3.4% of what is left. A small within-R^2 is normal and not damning on a noisy panel; headlining the inflated total R^2 (large simply because firms differ persistently) would be dishonest. The control coefficients pass an economic sanity check — bigger and more profitable firms disclose more — which is why I print them rather than bury them in a “Controls: Yes” row.
A final reading discipline: the 0.18 is a within-firm association. The firm fixed effects mean I am not claiming high-common-ownership firms disclose more than low-common-ownership ones (that between-firm comparison is confounded, and I make no claim about it); I am saying that as a given firm’s common ownership rises, its disclosure tends to rise too, net of market-wide quarter shocks. That is the comparison the design supports, and the comparison the verb “associated with” describes.


6. Robustness
The robustness checks are organized around the threats of Table 2, in the same order, each introduced as an answer to a doubt rather than a context-free extra regression. Before each, I state what a pass would look like, so I cannot redefine “pass” after seeing the number. All figures remain synthetic and illustrative.
Inference: does the result survive conservative clustering? A reader might worry that firm clustering understates dependence if residuals are also correlated across firms within a quarter (a common flow shock). Pass criterion: the estimate stays distinguishable from zero under the most conservative defensible clustering. Two-way clustering by firm and quarter widens the standard error from 0.061 to about 0.072 (the coefficient is unchanged at 0.18), giving t \approx 2.5, still significant at 5%; industry clustering (30 clusters) gives SE near 0.078, t \approx 2.3. With only 30 clusters the asymptotics are thin, so the honest statement is that the result is significant under every defensible clustering but with visibly wider intervals as I cluster more coarsely — not bulletproof, but not fragile on inference either.
Reverse causality: does lagging further change the story? A reader might worry that funds buy firms because they disclose more, so the arrow runs outcome → regressor. Pass criterion: the association is similar when ownership is lagged two quarters, which a pure reverse-causality story would weaken. The two-quarter lag yields about 0.16 (SE 0.064), close to the one-quarter estimate. This reduces but does not eliminate the concern: if funds anticipate disclosure two quarters ahead, even the deeper lag is contaminated.
Measurement: an artifact of one measure or the largest funds? A reader might worry that portfolio-weighted CO is sensitive to the giant index managers or to the “who is one manager” aggregation. Pass criterion: a differently constructed measure and a sample without the largest funds give the same sign and similar magnitude. Replacing CO with a count of common holders above a 1% stake (re-standardized) gives about 0.15 (SE 0.058); dropping the five largest managers before building CO gives about 0.17 (SE 0.063). Both are a touch smaller, consistent with the attenuation measurement error predicts, and both keep the sign and significance.
Industry-time shocks: do finer fixed effects kill it? A reader might worry that an industry-wide event moves peers’ ownership and a firm’s disclosure together within a quarter. Pass criterion: adding industry × quarter fixed effects, which absorb any shock common to an industry in a quarter, leaves the coefficient distinguishable from zero. This yields about 0.14 (SE 0.066), t \approx 2.1 — the most demanding specification in the paper, smaller but surviving at 5%. That some of the association is absorbed here is itself informative: part of the relationship operates at the industry-quarter level, exactly where a peer-group mechanism would live.
What does not survive — robustness is not identification. Every check above shows the number is stable; none of them shows the design is valid. This is the distinction a sophisticated reader cares about most. I can re-cluster, re-measure, and add finer fixed effects all day, and a time-varying firm-specific confounder — a firm getting more transparent for its own reasons and thereby more attractive to diversified funds — would survive every one of these checks intact, because the bias would be baked into the within-firm variation the design relies on. The honest one-line summary: the result is robust in the sense that it does not depend on arbitrary analytic choices, and not identified in the sense that I cannot rule out the confounder that would make it non-causal. I therefore add a firm-specific linear time trend as the closest I can come to addressing that confounder; it leaves the coefficient near 0.16 (SE 0.067), which bounds — but does not eliminate — a smooth firm trend. A non-linear or coincident trend remains the threat I cannot dispatch.
Figure 1 summarizes the point estimate and its 95% confidence interval across the six specifications, so a reader can see the stability and the widening intervals at a glance.
